How to Use This Book

This book is written so that you can prepare the whole of Section A of MTE 4101 without opening the lecture files. It is arranged by topic, not by year. Each chapter follows the same order:

  1. Theory: the content of Asief Sir's lectures (Process Field Instrumentations, Data Communication, Process control v3, Modified PID controllers, AJ CT2 solve, Recent Trends in Automation and Safety) rewritten as exam-ready paragraphs, tables and diagrams, plus the syllabus topics that the papers ask but the lecture files do not cover.
  2. Derivations: the blending-process model, block diagrams, offset analysis and flowmeter equations derived step by step.
  3. Solved past questions: every Section A question of the 2022, 2023 and 2024 term finals, quoted word for word with its year, number and marks, answered at the length the marks call for.

Sources and scope
Theory comes from Asief Sir's lecture files listed above; the Seborg, Edgar, Mellichamp & Doyle textbook Process Dynamics and Control (in the course folder) is used where the slides are silent (reset windup, DCS, fieldbus, HART). Industry 4.0, types of automation, the automation pyramid, PROFINET and SCADA are asked in the papers but are not in the lecture files; those answers are written from standard references (Groover, Automation, Production Systems and CIM; Bailey & Wright, Practical SCADA for Industry; PI specifications). The PLC questions of 2022 Section A belong to Priyo Sir's Section B material (W. Bolton, Programmable Logic Controllers). Past questions are from the KUET 4th Year 1st Term Examinations of 2022 (2k18 batch), 2023 (2k19 batch) and 2024 (2k20 batch).

1. Industrial Automation: Fundamentals, Types and the Automation Pyramid ★★★

Every Section A paper opens with this topic: what automation is, how it differs from mechanization, its types, its components, its economics and the automation pyramid. The answers are descriptive, so the marks go to clear definitions, well-chosen examples, a neat pyramid and comparison tables.

1.1 What Is Industrial Automation?

Definition (write this in the exam)
Industrial automation is the use of control systems — computers, PLCs, DCS, robots and information technologies — together with sensors and actuators to operate industrial machinery and processes with minimum human intervention. The control system measures what the process is doing, decides what to do and acts on the process automatically, so that production is carried out faster, more accurately, more safely and at lower cost than by hand.

The word comes from the Greek automatos (“acting by itself”). An automated system has three essential abilities:

  1. Sensing — sensors and transmitters measure process variables (temperature, pressure, flow, level, position, speed, presence of a part).
  2. Decision making — a controller (PLC, DCS, PAC, PC, embedded controller) compares the measurement with what is wanted and executes a control law or a logic sequence stored as a program.
  3. Actuation — final control elements (control valves, motors, drives, solenoids, cylinders, heaters) change the process.

Two kinds of automatic control are used in industry. Continuous (process) control keeps variables such as temperature or composition at a set point by feedback (Chapter 6); it is typical of the process industries (chemicals, oil and gas, power, water, food). Discrete (sequential) control switches devices on and off in a sequence — fill, heat, mix, drain; pick, place, weld — and is typical of manufacturing (automotive, electronics, packaging). Most plants use both.

1.2 Automation versus Mechanization

Mechanization is the use of machines to help or replace human muscle power, while a human still controls the machine. A lathe driven by an electric motor, a fork-lift truck or a power drill are mechanized: the machine supplies the energy, but the operator decides when to start, how far to feed and when to stop. Automation goes one step further and replaces human control and decision-making as well: the machine senses, decides and acts by itself according to a program.

AspectMechanizationAutomation
What is replacedHuman physical effort (muscle power)Human physical effort and human control, monitoring and decision-making
Role of the operatorOperates and controls the machine all the timeSupervises, sets targets, handles exceptions and maintenance
Feedback / sensingUsually none — the human closes the loop by watchingBuilt in: sensors and controllers close the loop automatically
ProgrammabilityNone; behaviour fixed by the machine designBehaviour set by a program (PLC, CNC, robot, DCS) and can be changed
ConsistencyDepends on operator skill and fatigueHigh and repeatable
ExamplesMotor-driven conveyor started by hand, power press operated by a pedal, tractorBottling line controlled by a PLC, CNC machining centre, robotic welding cell, boiler with automatic drum-level control
RelationMechanization is the first step; automation = mechanization + sensing + control logic.

1.3 Components of an Industrial Automation System

ComponentFunctionExamples
Sensors and transmittersDetect a physical quantity and convert it into a standard signal (4–20 mA, 24 V on/off, digital fieldbus) for the controller (Chapter 5).RTD, thermocouple, pressure transmitter, flowmeter, proximity switch, encoder, camera
ControllersThe “brain”: read inputs, execute the program or control algorithm (logic, PID, sequences, interlocks) and compute outputs.PLC, DCS controller, PAC, industrial PC, CNC, robot controller, RTU
Actuators / final control elementsConvert the controller output into physical action on the process.Control valve, VFD + motor, servo drive, solenoid valve, pneumatic cylinder, heater, contactor
Human–machine interface (HMI)Displays process status, alarms and trends; lets operators start/stop equipment and change set points.Touch panel, SCADA screens, operator station
Supervisory and information systemsCollect data from many controllers, log history, report, schedule production.SCADA, historian, MES, ERP
Industrial communication networkCarries data between field devices, controllers and computers (Chapter 3).PROFIBUS, PROFINET, Modbus, HART, EtherNet/IP, wireless
Power supply and safety systemProvides 24 V DC / AC power; protects people and plant.Power supplies, E-stop circuits, safety relays, light curtains, safety PLC
SoftwareProgramming, configuration, visualisation and data analysis.TIA Portal, ladder/FBD/ST programs, HMI and SCADA projects

1.4 Types of Automation

Automation is classified by how easily the system can be changed to make a different product. Groover's classical classification has three types, plus a fourth that integrates them:

The three types (Groover)
1. Fixed (hard) automation — the sequence of operations is fixed by the equipment configuration (cams, special tooling, transfer lines). Very high production rates of one product; changing the product needs a rebuild.
2. Programmable automation — the sequence is controlled by a program, so the equipment can be reprogrammed for a new product. Production is in batches; between batches the machine is stopped for reprogramming and new tooling (set-up time).
3. Flexible (soft) automation — an extension of programmable automation that changes over between products with almost no lost time (no batch set-up); different products can be made one after another in any mix.
4. Integrated automation — all machines, material handling and information systems of a plant are linked under computer control (CIM, Industry 4.0).
FeatureFixed automationProgrammable automationFlexible automation
Basic ideaSequence built into the hardwareSequence stored in a program; changed between batchesProgram changes on the fly; no set-up time between products
Production volumeVery high (mass production)Low to medium (batch production)Medium
Product varietyOne product (or very few)High — any product that can be programmedMedium — a family of similar products, mixed freely
ChangeoverVery difficult, costly re-toolingReprogramming + new tooling; lost production timeQuick, often automatic (tool changers, part programs downloaded)
InvestmentHigh initial cost of special equipmentHigh cost of general-purpose equipmentHighest — custom-engineered system
Cost per unitLowest (if volume is high)Relatively highMedium
ExamplesAutomobile engine-block transfer line, bottling machines, automatic assembly of light bulbs, paint-shop conveyorsCNC machine tools, industrial robots, PLC-controlled batch reactors, steel rolling millsFlexible manufacturing systems (FMS) of CNC machines with AGVs; robotic body-welding lines that build several car models in random order

1.5 Advantages, Disadvantages and the Economics of Automation

Advantages

  • Higher productivity and throughput; 24/7 operation.
  • Consistent, higher product quality; fewer defects and less scrap.
  • Lower labour cost per unit.
  • Better safety: machines do dangerous, hot, heavy or repetitive work.
  • Lower energy and material use through tight control.
  • Accurate data for traceability, maintenance and planning.
  • Shorter lead times and more flexibility (programmable systems).
  • Does tasks people cannot do (very fast, very precise, hazardous areas).

Disadvantages

  • High initial capital investment; long payback for small volumes.
  • Need for skilled engineers and technicians; training costs.
  • Displacement of low-skill jobs; social resistance.
  • Maintenance complexity; one failure can stop a whole line.
  • Less flexibility in fixed automation; risk of obsolescence.
  • Cyber-security risks once systems are networked.
  • Over-automation of an unstable process just makes bad parts faster.
Profit relation used in 2023 Q1(c)
Profit=Revenue−Total cost=(price×units sold)−(fixed cost+variable cost per unit×units)\text{Profit}=\text{Revenue}-\text{Total cost}=(\text{price}\times\text{units sold})-(\text{fixed cost}+\text{variable cost per unit}\times\text{units})Profit=Revenue−Total cost=(price×units sold)−(fixed cost+variable cost per unit×units) Automation raises profit by increasing revenue (more good units sold, higher quality → higher price and market share) and by reducing cost per unit (labour, scrap, energy, downtime, inventory).

1.6 The Automation Pyramid

The automation pyramid (based on the ISA-95 / IEC 62264 levels) shows how the devices and software of an automated plant are organised in levels. Going up, there are fewer devices, the data are more aggregated and the decisions are slower and more business-oriented; going down, there are many devices that must respond in real time.

LevelFunctionComponents
Level 0 — FieldPhysical interface with the process: measure and actuate.Sensors, transmitters, limit/proximity switches, control valves, motors, drives, solenoids
Level 1 — ControlReal-time control: logic, sequences, interlocks, PID loops.PLC, DCS controllers, PAC, RTU, CNC, robot controller
Level 2 — SupervisoryMonitoring and supervisory control of a plant area; alarms, trends, operator commands.SCADA, HMI panels, operator workstations, data historian
Level 3 — Plant management (MES)Production scheduling, recipe and quality management, tracking, performance (OEE).Manufacturing execution system, LIMS, maintenance management
Level 4 — Enterprise (ERP)Business planning: orders, purchasing, finance, logistics, HR.ERP software (e.g. SAP), corporate servers and cloud

Communication changes with the level: fast deterministic fieldbuses (PROFIBUS DP, PROFINET IO, IO-Link, HART) at levels 0–1, control networks / industrial Ethernet at levels 1–2, and office Ethernet / IT networks at levels 3–4. In Industry 4.0 the strict pyramid is becoming a network (IIoT devices can send data directly to the cloud), but the levels remain the standard way to describe an automation system.

1.7 Impact of Automation on the Manufacturing Industry

  • Productivity: machines run faster and continuously; cycle times fall; output per worker rises many times.
  • Quality and consistency: every part is made in the same way; in-line inspection catches defects immediately.
  • Cost structure: labour cost per unit falls; capital cost rises; economies of scale improve.
  • Safety and working conditions: dangerous, dirty and dull jobs are moved to machines.
  • Flexibility and customisation: programmable and flexible automation make small batches and product variants economic.
  • Workforce: fewer manual operators; more technicians, programmers, maintenance and data specialists.
  • Competitiveness: faster time to market, reliable delivery and traceability are now required by customers.

1.8 Solved Past Questions

2022 · Q2(a)What is industrial automation and how does it impact on the manufacturing industry? What are the key components of an industrial automation system? 12Topic: definition · impact · components

Industrial automation is the use of control systems (PLCs, DCS, computers, robots) and information technologies, together with sensors and actuators, to operate industrial machines and processes with minimum human intervention. The system senses the process, decides according to a stored program or control law, and acts on the process automatically. It covers continuous process control (e.g. temperature or level loops in a chemical plant) and discrete/sequential control (e.g. a PLC-controlled packaging line).

Impact on the manufacturing industry:

  1. Higher productivity: machines work faster and around the clock, so output per hour and per worker rises sharply.
  2. Better and consistent quality: processes are repeated identically; automatic inspection removes defects early, reducing scrap and rework.
  3. Lower production cost: labour, material waste and energy per unit fall; the cost structure moves from labour to capital.
  4. Improved safety: robots and automatic machines take over hazardous operations (welding, painting, heavy lifting, toxic or hot areas).
  5. Flexibility: programmable systems allow quick product changes and customised products.
  6. Data and traceability: every step is recorded, supporting quality certification, maintenance planning and continuous improvement.
  7. Workforce change: fewer manual jobs, more demand for skilled technicians, programmers and engineers.
  8. Competitiveness: shorter lead times and reliable delivery let manufacturers compete globally.

Key components (Fig. 1.1):

  1. Sensors and transmitters — measure temperature, pressure, flow, level, position, presence; convert to standard signals (4–20 mA, 24 V DC, fieldbus).
  2. Controllers — PLC, DCS, PAC, industrial PC, CNC or robot controller; execute the logic and control algorithms.
  3. Actuators / final control elements — control valves, motors with drives, solenoid valves, cylinders, heaters.
  4. Human–machine interface (HMI) — panels and screens for operators to monitor and command the process.
  5. Supervisory and information systems — SCADA, historian, MES and ERP for supervision, data logging and planning.
  6. Communication networks — fieldbuses and industrial Ethernet (PROFIBUS, PROFINET, Modbus, HART) linking all devices.
  7. Power supply and safety systems — 24 V DC supplies, emergency stops, safety relays and guards.
  8. Software — controller programs, HMI/SCADA configuration and data-analysis tools.
Source lectureAsief Sir · Process Field Instrumentation (Process Field Instrumentations_Ver 1.2.pdf, p. 6); Data Communication (Data Communication.pdf, p. 1) — only the loop elements and node types are on the slides; definition and impact on manufacturing — see §1.1, §1.7

2023 · Q1(a)What is meant by industrial automation? How does it differ from mechanization? 06Topic: automation vs mechanization

Industrial automation is the use of control systems such as PLCs, DCS, computers and robots, with sensors and actuators, to operate industrial processes and machines with minimum human intervention: the system measures, decides by a program and acts by itself.

Difference from mechanization: mechanization uses machines to replace human muscle power, but a human still controls them; automation also replaces human control and decision-making.

PointMechanizationAutomation
ReplacesPhysical effort onlyPhysical effort + control and decisions
ControlManual, by the operatorAutomatic, by a program/controller
FeedbackHuman eyes and judgementSensors and controllers (closed loop)
Human roleOperatorSupervisor / programmer

2023 · Q1(b)Briefly explain different types of industrial automation with proper example. 12Topic: types of automation

Industrial automation is classified into four types (§1.4):

  1. Fixed (hard) automation. The sequence of processing or assembly operations is fixed by the equipment configuration (special tooling, cams, transfer mechanisms). Each operation is simple, but the integration of many of them in one machine gives very high production rates. Features: high initial investment in custom equipment, very high output, lowest unit cost, but very little flexibility for product change.
    Example: automobile engine-block transfer lines; automatic bottling and capping machines; machines that assemble light bulbs or ball-pen refills.
  2. Programmable automation. The equipment can change its sequence of operations to suit a new product; the sequence is controlled by a program (coded instructions). Products are made in batches; between batches the system is reprogrammed and re-tooled, which costs set-up time. Features: high investment in general-purpose equipment, lower production rate, flexibility to cope with changes in product configuration.
    Example: CNC machine tools, industrial robots, PLC-controlled batch reactors, steel rolling mills.
  3. Flexible (soft) automation. An extension of programmable automation that can produce a variety of products (a part family) with virtually no time lost for changeover; reprogramming is done off-line and parts are changed automatically. Features: high investment in a custom-engineered system, continuous production of a variable mix of products, medium production rates.
    Example: flexible manufacturing systems (FMS) — CNC machining centres served by robots and automated guided vehicles; car body-welding lines that build several models in any order.
  4. Integrated automation. Complete automation of a plant in which machines, material handling, inspection and information flow are all coordinated by computers under a single control system (computer-integrated manufacturing, CIM; today Industry 4.0).
    Example: a fully automated semiconductor fab or automobile factory linked from ERP orders down to robot programs.

Fig. 1.2 summarises the first three types on a production-volume / product-variety chart.

2023 · Q1(c)The main purpose of a company is to make profit. How does automation increases profit? Explain. 10Topic: economics of automation

Profit = revenue − total cost. Automation increases profit by raising revenue and lowering cost per unit:

  1. Higher productivity: automated machines run faster and 24 hours a day with few stops. More units are produced from the same plant, so fixed costs (building, equipment, management) are spread over more units and revenue rises.
  2. Lower labour cost: fewer operators are needed per unit; one technician can supervise several machines.
  3. Better quality, less scrap and rework: repeatable processes and automatic inspection reduce rejected products, warranty claims and returns; raw material is not wasted.
  4. Higher price and market share: consistent quality, reliable delivery and traceability let the company sell at a better price and win more customers.
  5. Lower energy and material consumption: tight control (e.g. exact dosing, optimum temperature) saves fuel, power and ingredients.
  6. Less downtime: automatic monitoring, alarms and predictive maintenance keep machines available.
  7. Lower inventory and shorter lead time: faster, predictable production means less work-in-progress and less capital tied up in stock.
  8. Fewer accidents: fewer injuries reduce compensation, insurance and lost-time costs.
  9. Flexibility: programmable automation makes small batches and product variants economic, opening new markets.
Illustration
If automation raises output from 1 000 to 1 500 units/day and cuts the cost per unit from Tk 80 to Tk 65 while the selling price stays Tk 100, the daily profit rises from 1 000 × (100 − 80) = Tk 20 000 to 1 500 × (100 − 65) = Tk 52 500 (before paying for the investment). The extra profit pays back the automation investment over time.

2023 · Q1(d)Draw the automation pyramid mentioning all its levels and related components. 07Topic: automation pyramid
  • Level 0 – Field level: sensors, transmitters, switches, actuators, control valves, motors and drives that are in direct contact with the process.
  • Level 1 – Control level: PLCs, DCS controllers, PACs and RTUs that read the field signals and execute logic and PID control in real time.
  • Level 2 – Supervisory level: SCADA and HMI systems, operator stations and the historian for monitoring, alarms and set-point changes.
  • Level 3 – Plant management (MES): production scheduling, quality and recipe management, tracking and plant performance.
  • Level 4 – Enterprise level (ERP): business planning — orders, purchasing, finance and logistics.

Moving up the pyramid there are fewer devices and more aggregated information with slower time scales; moving down there are more devices with faster, real-time response.

2. Industry 4.0, Recent Trends and Safety in Automation ★★★

This chapter covers the “modern” part of the syllabus: the fourth industrial revolution (written as Industrial 4.0 on the 2022 paper — the usual name is Industry 4.0), the recent trends listed in the lecture Recent Trends in Automation and Safety, and the machine-safety measures from the same lecture.

2.1 The Four Industrial Revolutions

Definition: Industry 4.0
Industry 4.0 (the fourth industrial revolution, the term launched in Germany in 2011) is the digital transformation of manufacturing in which machines, products, people and information systems are connected through cyber-physical systems (CPS) and the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT). Real-time data from the shop floor are analysed (cloud, edge, AI) and used to let the factory monitor itself, make decentralised decisions and adapt automatically — the smart factory.

2.2 Key Components and Technologies of Industry 4.0

TechnologyWhat it does in a smart factory
Cyber-physical systems (CPS)Physical machines with embedded computing and communication; each machine has a digital representation and can exchange data and make local decisions.
Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT)Connects sensors, machines and devices so they communicate and share data; enables condition monitoring, inventory tracking and predictive maintenance.
Big data and analyticsCollect and analyse large volumes of production data to find causes of defects, optimise energy and throughput.
Artificial intelligence and machine learningLearn from data to predict failures, detect defects in real time (machine vision), optimise processes.
Cloud and edge computingCloud: scalable storage and computing for plant-wide data. Edge: processing close to the machine for low latency and security.
Digital twin and simulationVirtual replica of a machine, line or process used to design, test (virtual commissioning) and optimise before acting on the real plant.
Autonomous and collaborative robotsCobots working beside humans; autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) moving material without fixed tracks.
Additive manufacturing3D printing for rapid prototyping, spare parts and customised products with less material waste.
Augmented and virtual realityAR overlays instructions on real equipment for maintenance; VR provides immersive training.
Horizontal and vertical integrationVertical: field devices → PLC → SCADA → MES → ERP share data seamlessly. Horizontal: the whole value chain (suppliers, factory, customers) is connected.
CybersecurityProtects connected systems: network segmentation, encryption, authentication, audits.
5G / industrial wirelessLow-latency, reliable wireless links for mobile machines and massive numbers of IIoT sensors.

2.3 Conventional Production versus Industry 4.0

AspectConventional (Industry 3.0) productionIndustry 4.0 production
Control structureCentralised, hierarchical automation pyramid; islands of automationDecentralised: smart machines and products communicate and decide locally
DataLittle data collected; used late, mostly for reportsReal-time data from every device; analytics and AI turn it into decisions
ConnectivityMachines isolated or on closed fieldbusesEverything connected (IIoT, cloud, 5G); vertical and horizontal integration
Product varietyMass production of standard productsMass customisation — batch size one at mass-production cost
MaintenanceReactive (after failure) or fixed-interval preventivePredictive, based on condition monitoring and machine learning
Design and commissioningPhysical prototypes, trial and error on the real plantSimulation and digital twins; virtual commissioning
Quality controlSampling inspection at the end of the line100 % in-line inspection (vision + AI), automatic correction
Human roleOperator performing repetitive tasks; robots caged awaySupervisor, problem-solver and collaborator with cobots, supported by AR
FlexibilityLow; changeovers costlyHigh; self-configuring, reconfigurable lines

2.4 Benefits and Challenges of Implementing Industry 4.0

Benefits

  • Higher productivity and equipment effectiveness (OEE).
  • Better quality through real-time monitoring and AI inspection.
  • Less unplanned downtime (predictive maintenance).
  • Mass customisation and faster time to market.
  • Lower energy use and waste; sustainability.
  • Transparency and traceability across the supply chain.
  • Safer work: dangerous tasks to robots; remote monitoring.
  • New data-driven business models (product-as-a-service).

Challenges

  • High investment; uncertain return for small and medium firms.
  • Integration of old (legacy) machines and incompatible protocols.
  • Cybersecurity threats on connected plants.
  • Shortage of skilled workers; need for retraining.
  • Data ownership, privacy and standardisation issues.
  • Reliable high-speed networks needed (infrastructure).
  • Organisational change and resistance of workforce.
  • Complexity of managing huge amounts of data.

2.5 Impact on the Workforce and Required Skills

Industry 4.0 automates routine manual and routine cognitive tasks (repetitive assembly, manual inspection, data entry), so these jobs shrink. At the same time it creates new jobs — automation and robotics technicians, PLC/IIoT programmers, data analysts, digital-twin engineers, cybersecurity specialists — and changes existing jobs from operating machines to supervising, maintaining and improving them. Skills therefore shift toward:

  • Technical: PLC and robot programming, mechatronics, industrial networks, IIoT and cloud platforms, data analytics and AI/ML, cybersecurity, simulation and digital twins, additive manufacturing.
  • Cognitive: systems thinking, complex problem solving, decision making with data.
  • Social and personal: collaboration in interdisciplinary teams, communication, adaptability and lifelong learning.

2.6 Human–Machine Collaboration

In conventional production, people and machines work separately: machines provide power, speed and repetition; humans load, operate, inspect and decide. Industrial robots work inside fenced cells because they are not safe near people. In Industry 4.0, humans and machines work together: collaborative robots share the workspace (power and force limiting, speed and separation monitoring, ISO/TS 15066), AR glasses guide operators step by step, exoskeletons reduce strain, and AI systems give decision support. The machine does what it does best (strength, precision, endurance, data processing); the human does what people do best (judgement, dexterity on varied tasks, creativity, handling exceptions).

2.7 Recent Trends in Industrial Automation (lecture list)

#TrendKey idea (lecture)
1Robotics and cobotsCollaborative robots work alongside humans, are easily programmable and adaptable; AMRs move material without rigid infrastructure.
2AI and machine learningMachines learn from data: optimise processes, predict maintenance, detect defects in real time.
3Internet of ThingsConnects machines, sensors and devices to share data; equipment health, inventory tracking, predictive maintenance.
4Digital twinsVirtual replica of a physical asset or process; simulate and analyse before implementation, risk-free.
5AR and VRAR overlays digital information on the real equipment for maintenance and troubleshooting; VR gives immersive training.
6Edge computingData processed close to the source; low latency, better security, uninterrupted operation.
7Additive manufacturing3D printing: rapid prototyping, customisation, less waste, complex light structures.
8Sustainable automationLower energy use, less waste, recycling, lower carbon footprint.
9CybersecurityManufacturing was the most attacked sector in 2024 (over 25 % of incidents); segmentation, encryption, audits.
105G connectivityFast, reliable, low-latency wireless for real-time monitoring and many IoT devices.

2.8 Safety in Automated Machinery

The first priority in designing automated machinery is the safety of personnel; protection of the machine itself comes second. Moving parts, hot surfaces, caustic substances and sharp edges are the typical hazards, and national/regional standards (e.g. IEC 60204-1, ISO 13849, OSHA) set the rules. The lecture lists six ways of safeguarding operators:

  1. Emergency stop (E-stop) circuits — stop categories 0, 1 and 2 (table below). The E-stop is a category 0 stop with only mechanical removal of power; no software may be involved.
  2. Physical guarding — the simplest method: a cover or barrier between hazard and operator; removable only with a tool, or if hinged, fitted with a safety (interlock) switch, possibly with a guard-locking mechanism.
  3. Lockout/tagout (LOTO) — protects workers from hazardous energy during maintenance: a lock secures the energy-isolating device and a tag warns others not to operate the equipment.
  4. Design mitigation — design safety into the machine: rounded corners, moving parts placed out of reach; usually the cheapest solution.
  5. Guard devices — light curtains (invisible infrared barrier that stops the machine when broken) and safety laser (floor) scanners that monitor a flexible protective zone.
  6. Intrinsic safety — equipment for flammable atmospheres designed so that it cannot store or release enough energy to create an igniting spark or hot surface.
Stop category (IEC 60204-1)ActionTypical use
0Uncontrolled stop: power to the actuators removed immediatelyEmergency stop (hard-wired)
1Controlled stop with power available to brake the actuators; power removed when stoppedLarge inertia drives, spindles
2Controlled stop with power left available to the actuatorsNormal stop / pause, position holding

2022 · Q1(b)Discuss the benefits and challenges associated with the implementation of Industrial 4.0 in industries. Provide examples to support your answer. 10Topic: Industry 4.0 benefits and challenges

Benefits (with examples):

  1. Higher productivity and efficiency. Connected machines and real-time scheduling raise OEE. Example: the Siemens electronics plant at Amberg runs highly automated, data-driven lines and is widely reported to achieve a quality rate of about 99.99 %.
  2. Predictive maintenance and less downtime. Vibration and temperature data analysed by machine learning predict failures before they occur. Example: gas-turbine and wind-turbine makers monitor their fleets online and schedule repairs before breakdowns.
  3. Better quality. AI vision systems inspect every part in real time instead of sampling. Example: automotive paint shops use cameras and AI to detect paint defects automatically.
  4. Mass customisation and speed. Flexible, digitally controlled lines make individual products economically. Example: Harley-Davidson's reconfigured York plant is reported to have cut its build-to-order cycle from about 21 days to 6 hours.
  5. Lower cost of design and commissioning. Digital twins test changes virtually. Example: virtual commissioning of a PLC program on a simulated conveyor line before installation.
  6. Energy saving and sustainability through monitoring of every consumer.
  7. Supply-chain transparency — orders, stock and production status visible in real time.

Challenges (with examples):

  1. High initial investment in sensors, networks, software and training — difficult for small and medium enterprises, e.g. a local garment factory.
  2. Legacy equipment and interoperability: old machines without communication and different vendor protocols must be retrofitted with gateways (OPC UA).
  3. Cybersecurity: connected plants become targets; e.g. ransomware attacks have halted production lines, and manufacturing was the most attacked sector in 2024.
  4. Skills gap: workers need data, IT and automation skills; retraining is costly.
  5. Data management and standards: huge data volumes, ownership and privacy questions.
  6. Infrastructure: reliable power and high-speed networks (5G, fibre) are needed — a real constraint in developing countries.
  7. Organisational resistance and fear of job loss.
Source lectureAsief Sir · Recent Trends in Automation and Safety (Recent Trends in Automation and Safety.pdf, pp. 1–2) — benefits and challenges of Industry 4.0 as such are not on the slides — see §2.4

Impacts on the workforce and job market:

  1. Job displacement: routine manual jobs (repetitive assembly, packing, material handling, manual inspection) and routine clerical jobs are automated.
  2. Job creation: new roles appear — robotics and automation technicians, PLC/IIoT programmers, data scientists, digital-twin and simulation engineers, cybersecurity specialists, AR/VR content developers.
  3. Job transformation: operators become supervisors and problem-solvers; maintenance becomes predictive and data-based.
  4. Polarisation: demand grows for high-skill jobs while low-skill jobs decline, which can widen wage gaps unless workers are retrained.
  5. Safer and more ergonomic work: cobots, exoskeletons and remote monitoring reduce dangerous and strenuous tasks.
  6. Flexible and remote work: plants can be monitored and serviced remotely.
  7. Need for lifelong learning: technologies change quickly, so continuous up-skilling becomes part of the job.

2022 · Q1(d)Evaluate the role of human-machine collaboration in both conventional industrial production and Industrial 4.0. 05Topic: human–machine collaboration

Conventional production: humans and machines are separated. Machines provide power, speed and repetition; humans operate, load, inspect and make every decision. Robots work in fenced cells for safety. Collaboration is limited to the operator controlling the machine through push buttons and panels; the human is the flexible, intelligent part of the system but also the source of variation and fatigue errors.

Industry 4.0: humans and machines work together in shared spaces:

  • Cobots work beside people without fences (force/speed limiting), taking the heavy or repetitive part of a task while the human does the delicate or variable part.
  • AR/VR guide operators and maintenance staff with digital instructions and give safe training.
  • AI decision support analyses data and suggests actions; the human makes the final judgement.
  • Exoskeletons and assistive devices reduce strain.

Evaluation: collaboration in Industry 4.0 combines machine precision and endurance with human judgement and creativity, giving higher productivity, flexibility, quality and better ergonomics. It requires new safety standards, trust in the technology and new skills; the human role shifts from manual operator to supervisor and problem-solver rather than disappearing.

Source lectureAsief Sir · Recent Trends in Automation and Safety (Recent Trends in Automation and Safety.pdf, p. 1) — only collaborative robots are on the slide — see §2.6
2024 · Q1(c)Write short notes on the following safety measures. (i) Emergency stop, (ii) Physical guarding, and (iii) Lockout/tagout 09Topic: machine safety

(i) Emergency stop (E-stop). An E-stop is a manually operated device (a red mushroom-head push button on a yellow background, or a pull cord) that brings a machine to a stop as quickly as possible when a person is in danger. Stop functions are classified as:

  • Category 0 — uncontrolled stop by immediately removing power to the machine actuators;
  • Category 1 — controlled stop with power available to the actuators to achieve the stop, then power removed;
  • Category 2 — controlled stop with power left available to the actuators.

The E-stop circuit is a category 0 stop with only mechanical (hard-wired) removal of circuit power — no software may be involved. The button uses normally-closed contacts (a broken wire also stops the machine), latches when pressed and must be reset deliberately before the machine can restart.

(ii) Physical guarding. The simplest safety method: a cover, fence or other physical barrier is placed between the hazard (moving parts, hot surfaces, sharp edges) and the operator. A fixed guard must be removable only with a tool; a hinged guard (door) must have a safety interlock switch that stops the machine when the guard is opened. Safety switches with guard-locking keep the door locked until the machine is in a safe state (released only by an E-stop condition if the hazard analysis requires).

(iii) Lockout/tagout (LOTO). A procedure that protects workers from hazardous energy (electrical, pneumatic, hydraulic, mechanical, thermal) while machines are serviced or maintained. A lockout device (padlock) secures the energy-isolating device (breaker, valve) in the off position, and a tagout device (tag) warns others not to operate the equipment. Typical steps: notify → shut down → isolate all energy sources → apply personal lock and tag → release stored energy → verify zero energy (try to start) → do the work → remove locks only by the person who applied them.

Source lectureAsief Sir · Recent Trends in Automation and Safety (Recent Trends in Automation and Safety.pdf, p. 3)
2024 · Q1(d)How are the following trends influencing traditional industrial automation systems? (i) Digital twins (ii) AR and VR (iii) Edge computing 09Topic: recent trends

(i) Digital twins. A digital twin is a virtual replica of a physical asset or process, kept updated with live data. Influence on traditional automation:

  • Production processes are simulated and analysed before implementation; PLC programs can be tested by virtual commissioning, so start-up time and errors on site fall.
  • Design and process optimisation are done in a risk-free virtual environment instead of trial and error on the real line.
  • Comparing the twin with live data supports predictive maintenance and “what-if” studies for operators.

(ii) AR and VR. Augmented reality overlays digital information (instructions, live values, wiring diagrams) onto the real equipment; virtual reality creates a fully simulated environment.

  • AR helps technicians identify and repair equipment faster — maintenance and troubleshooting no longer rely on paper manuals.
  • Remote experts can see what the technician sees and guide the repair.
  • VR gives immersive, safe training of operators and engineers on dangerous or expensive plants, improving skills and reducing errors.

(iii) Edge computing. Data are processed close to their source (near sensors and machines) instead of only in central cloud servers.

  • Real-time analysis and decisions with low latency — essential for control and fast quality inspection.
  • Less data sent to the cloud, lower bandwidth cost, and sensitive data stay on site (better security).
  • Operation continues even if the cloud link fails (uninterrupted operations); edge devices add analytics to traditional PLC-based systems without replacing them.
Source lectureAsief Sir · Recent Trends in Automation and Safety (Recent Trends in Automation and Safety.pdf, p. 1)

3. Industrial Data Communication, Networks and Fieldbuses ★★★

Automation devices are useless in isolation: sensors, controllers, drives, HMIs and computers must exchange data. This chapter follows the lecture Data Communication (network terms, topologies, media, connectors, switch and router) and adds the protocols that the papers ask about: PROFIBUS, Ethernet/PROFINET and HART.

3.1 Data Communication and Why Automation Needs It

Definitions (lecture)
Data communication is the transfer of information from one point to another. Industrial automation provides interconnection between devices (sensors, actuators, controllers and PCs) and enables communication between them. When two or more devices are connected for data exchange, it is called a network. Any communication system needs a transmitter to send information, a receiver to accept it, and a link between the two.

Industrial automation needs data communication because:

  1. Control: field measurements must reach the controller and controller outputs must reach the actuators — reliably and in real time.
  2. Coordination: several PLCs, drives and robots on one line must be synchronised (interlocks, recipes, sequences).
  3. Monitoring and supervision: HMI and SCADA need live data and alarms from the whole plant, often from remote sites.
  4. Less wiring: one bus cable replaces hundreds of point-to-point 4–20 mA and 24 V wires, reducing cost, installation time and faults.
  5. Diagnostics and maintenance: smart devices report their health, calibration and faults over the network (HART, fieldbus).
  6. Configuration: devices can be set up and calibrated remotely.
  7. Integration with business systems: production data flow to MES/ERP for scheduling, quality and traceability (vertical integration, Industry 4.0).

3.2 Basic Network Terms

TermMeaning (lecture)
NodeEach device on a network. In an industrial network a node can be a controller (PLC, PAC or DCS), a field device (sensor/transmitter or actuator), an HMI, a server or a workstation.
Network mediaThe channel of communication used to interconnect nodes: copper twisted-pair, copper coaxial and fibre-optic cables (wired networks), and radio waves — Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, cellular (wireless networks).
ProtocolThe agreed structure in which devices communicate — how data are encoded, framed, addressed, timed and checked, so that the receiver understands what the transmitter sends.
Network topologyHow the nodes are arranged and interconnected. Physical topology: the physical layout of nodes and cables. Logical topology: how data actually flow through the network, based on how the protocol works.
HubA simple connector that joins wires from different directions; works only on the physical layer and repeats every signal to all ports.
SwitchConnects devices (PLCs, HMIs, PCs) in a network; works at the data-link layer (OSI layer 2) using MAC addresses and forwards each packet only to the port of the destination device.
RouterConnects multiple switches and their networks to form a larger network; works with IP addresses (layer 3); devices networked via a switch can reach the internet through a router.

3.3 Network Topologies

  • Point-to-point: a single link between two devices — e.g. a PLC connected to a PC to download a program, or a PLC connected to an HMI.
  • Bus: every node is connected to one cable segment called the trunk, backbone or bus, with termination resistors at both ends to improve signal quality (prevent reflections). Data sent by one node reach all nodes, but only the addressed node accepts them — like a teacher calling one student's name in a class. Example: PLCs, HMIs and remote I/O on PROFIBUS. Cheap and simple, but a cable break can split the network.
  • Star: every node is connected to a central switch, router or hub; nodes communicate indirectly through it. Example: Ethernet/PROFINET. Easy to add nodes and isolate faults, but the central device is a single point of failure.
  • Ring: nodes connected in a closed loop; data pass from node to node until they reach the destination. Redundant rings (e.g. PROFINET MRP) keep working if one link breaks.
  • Others: tree (hierarchy of stars/buses) and mesh (many paths, used in WirelessHART).

3.4 Network Media, Cables, Connectors and Devices

CableConstruction and useConnector(s)
Twisted-pair copper (CAT5e, CAT6)Pairs of insulated copper wires twisted to cancel noise; unshielded (UTP) or shielded (STP). Standard medium of Ethernet/PROFINET up to 100 m per segment, 100 Mbit/s – 1 Gbit/s.RJ45 (Registered Jack 45); M12 (industrial IP67)
Coaxial copper (e.g. RG59)Centre conductor, dielectric, braided shield and jacket; good noise immunity; used for video (CCTV) and older networks.BNC (Bayonet Neill–Concelman); F-type
Fibre-optic cableGlass core and cladding carrying light; single-mode or multimode; immune to EMI, long distance (km), high bandwidth, electrically isolating.SC, ST, LC, FC

Connectors named in the lecture
BNC for coaxial cables · PROFIBUS connector for PROFIBUS cables · RJ45 for twisted-pair CAT5/CAT6 cables. Network connectors terminate a cable segment and attach the medium to hubs, switches, routers, controllers and PCs.

3.5 Layered Model of Communication (OSI) — Short Note

LayerNameJobIndustrial example
7ApplicationServices to the user program (read/write variables, alarms)PROFIBUS DP services, PROFINET IO, HART commands
6, 5Presentation, sessionData format, dialogue control(usually empty in fieldbuses)
4, 3Transport, networkEnd-to-end delivery, routing by IP addressTCP/UDP, IP (routers)
2Data linkFraming, MAC addressing, bus access, error checkEthernet MAC (switch), PROFIBUS FDL (token + master/slave)

Fieldbuses use only layers 1, 2 and 7 to keep them fast and deterministic.

3.6 Fieldbuses: PROFIBUS, Ethernet and PROFINET

A fieldbus is a digital, serial, two-way communication network that connects field devices (sensors, actuators, drives, remote I/O) with controllers, replacing individual analog wiring. The main standards are collected in IEC 61158.

3.6.1 PROFIBUS (Process Field Bus)

  • Origin and standard: German fieldbus (1989), now IEC 61158 / IEC 61784, maintained by PROFIBUS & PROFINET International (PI). Widely used in factory and process automation, especially with Siemens PLCs.
  • Versions: PROFIBUS DP (Decentralised Periphery) — fast cyclic exchange between a controller and distributed I/O, drives, valve islands; PROFIBUS PA (Process Automation) — for process instruments, MBP physical layer (IEC 61158-2) at 31.25 kbit/s, power and data on the same two wires, intrinsically safe for hazardous areas; (PROFIBUS FMS, the original peer-to-peer version, is obsolete).
  • Physical layer (DP): RS-485 shielded twisted pair, line (bus) topology, terminating resistors at both ends; 9.6 kbit/s to 12 Mbit/s (segment length about 1200 m at ≤ 93.75 kbit/s down to 100 m at 12 Mbit/s); up to 32 stations per segment, 126 addresses (0–125) with repeaters; optional fibre optics.
  • Bus access: hybrid — token passing among master stations, and master–slave polling between a master and its slaves. Class 1 master = PLC (cyclic data); class 2 master = engineering/diagnostic tool.
  • Device integration: every device is described by a GSD file imported into the configuration tool.
  • Data: up to 244 bytes of I/O data per slave per cycle; cyclic I/O plus acyclic parameter and diagnostic services.

3.6.2 Ethernet for Industrial Communication

  • Ethernet (IEEE 802.3) is the standard LAN technology: frames contain a preamble, destination and source MAC addresses, type field, 46–1500 bytes of data and a CRC check. Original Ethernet used a shared bus with CSMA/CD (carrier sense multiple access with collision detection), which is not deterministic.
  • Modern industrial Ethernet uses switched, full-duplex star/line/ring topologies at 100 Mbit/s – 1 Gbit/s, so collisions are eliminated; priority tagging (IEEE 802.1Q) and time synchronisation (IEEE 1588) give predictable timing.
  • Hardware is ruggedised: DIN-rail managed switches, IP67 M12 connectors, shielded CAT5e/CAT6 cables, fibre for long or noisy runs; wide temperature ranges.
  • Higher layers: TCP/IP and UDP for configuration, HMI, web servers and IT integration; real-time protocols on top — PROFINET, EtherNet/IP, Modbus TCP, EtherCAT.
  • Advantages: high speed and bandwidth, one network from field to office (vertical integration), cheap standard components, wireless (Wi-Fi) extension, remote access. Drawbacks: plain Ethernet is not deterministic and is exposed to IT security threats.

3.6.3 PROFINET

  • PROFINET (Process Field Net) is the open industrial Ethernet standard of PI (IEC 61158/61784), the Ethernet successor of PROFIBUS.
  • Devices: IO controller (PLC running the program), IO devices (remote I/O, drives, valve terminals, robots), IO supervisor (HMI/engineering tool). Devices are described by GSDML (XML) files and identified by a device name, MAC and IP address.
  • Communication channels: standard TCP/IP (non-real-time: configuration, diagnostics, web; ~100 ms); RT (real time: cyclic I/O data directly on the Ethernet layer, bypassing TCP/IP; cycle times ≈ 1–10 ms); IRT (isochronous real time: hardware-scheduled time slots, cycle ≤ 1 ms with jitter below 1 µs, for motion control).
  • Network: 100 Mbit/s full duplex (switched), star, line, tree or ring topology (Media Redundancy Protocol), copper (RJ45/M12, ≤ 100 m per segment), fibre or wireless; practically unlimited number of devices.
  • Communication model: provider–consumer — each device sends its data cyclically without being polled.
  • Integration: existing PROFIBUS segments are connected through proxies; PROFIsafe gives safety communication over the same cable.
FeaturePROFIBUS DPPROFINET IO
BasisSerial fieldbus (RS-485)Industrial Ethernet (IEEE 802.3)
Speed9.6 kbit/s – 12 Mbit/s, half duplex100 Mbit/s (1 Gbit/s) full duplex
Access methodToken passing + master–slave pollingProvider–consumer on switched Ethernet
Number of devicesMax. 126 addresses (32 per segment)Practically unlimited
Data per device≤ 244 bytes≤ 1440 bytes per frame
TopologyLine (bus) with terminatorsStar, line, tree, ring (redundant)
AddressingStation address set on the deviceDevice name + IP/MAC address
Device fileGSDGSDML (XML)
Cable / connectorViolet shielded twisted pair, 9-pin D-subCAT5e/CAT6, RJ45/M12, fibre
Real-time performanceCycle depends on number of slaves and baud rateRT ≈ 1–10 ms; IRT ≤ 1 ms, jitter < 1 µs
IT integration / wirelessNo (needs gateway); no wirelessYes — TCP/IP, web server, Wi-Fi possible
DiagnosticsLimitedExtensive (topology, port statistics, web)

3.7 HART Protocol

HART (Highway Addressable Remote Transducer) is an open, hybrid analog + digital protocol, developed by Rosemount in the 1980s and now managed by the FieldComm Group. The lecture lists HART, BRAIN and FOUNDATION Fieldbus as digital signals a transmitter can use besides 4–20 mA. Its key idea is to superimpose a digital signal on the ordinary 4–20 mA loop so that both travel on the same two wires.

  • Signalling: Bell 202 frequency-shift keying (FSK): logic 1 = 1200 Hz, logic 0 = 2200 Hz, amplitude ±0.5 mA, bit rate 1200 bit/s. The FSK sine wave averages to zero, so the analog 4–20 mA value is not disturbed.
  • Two channels at once: the analog current carries the primary variable continuously for control; the digital channel carries extra variables (secondary, third and fourth variables), configuration, calibration, range, tag, device status and diagnostics.
  • Master–slave: the field device is a slave and answers requests. Up to two masters: primary master (DCS/PLC with HART input card or modem) and secondary master (hand-held communicator or laptop). About two transactions per second; in burst mode the device sends data continuously without being polled.
  • Modes: point-to-point (one device, analog + digital) and multidrop (up to 15 devices in HART 5, 63 in HART 6/7 on one pair, each with a polling address; the current is fixed at 4 mA, so only digital data are used).
  • Loop resistance: at least 250 Ω in the loop is needed so that the ±0.5 mA FSK current produces a readable voltage.
  • WirelessHART (IEC 62591): 2.4 GHz self-organising mesh network for the same devices.

Advantages: uses existing 4–20 mA wiring and instruments; remote configuration and diagnostics; extra process variables; compatible with analog-only systems; simple and widely supported. Limitations: slow (1200 bit/s), so digital data are not suitable for fast control.

3.8 Solved Past Questions

2022 · Q4(a)Describe PROFIBUS and Ethernet protocol for industrial communication. 10Topic: PROFIBUS · industrial Ethernet

PROFIBUS (Process Field Bus) is an open fieldbus standard (IEC 61158) originating in Germany, used to connect PLCs with distributed field devices (Fig. 3.2).

  • Variants: PROFIBUS DP (Decentralised Periphery) for fast cyclic data exchange between a PLC and remote I/O, drives and valve islands; PROFIBUS PA (Process Automation) for process instruments — 31.25 kbit/s, power and data on the same two wires, intrinsically safe for hazardous areas.
  • Physical layer: RS-485 shielded twisted-pair cable in a bus (line) topology with terminating resistors at both ends; 9.6 kbit/s to 12 Mbit/s; up to 32 stations per segment and 126 addresses with repeaters; fibre optics for long distances.
  • Access method: token passing between masters and master–slave polling of slaves; class 1 master = PLC, class 2 master = engineering tool. Each device is integrated with its GSD file.
  • Data: cyclic I/O (up to 244 bytes per slave) plus acyclic parameter and diagnostic data.
  • Advantages: deterministic, proven, reduces wiring, rich diagnostics, many vendors. Limitations: limited speed and number of devices, needs correct termination, no direct IT integration.

Ethernet (IEEE 802.3) is the LAN technology adapted for industry as industrial Ethernet:

  • Frame: preamble, destination and source MAC addresses, type, 46–1500 data bytes, CRC; TCP/IP or UDP/IP above it.
  • Access: classic Ethernet uses CSMA/CD on a shared medium, which is non-deterministic; industrial Ethernet uses switched full-duplex links (no collisions), priority tagging (802.1Q) and clock synchronisation (IEEE 1588) to make timing predictable.
  • Physical layer: 100 Mbit/s – 1 Gbit/s over CAT5e/CAT6 twisted pair (RJ45 or rugged M12 connectors, ≤ 100 m) or fibre; star, line or ring topology with managed industrial switches.
  • Industrial protocols on Ethernet: PROFINET, EtherNet/IP, Modbus TCP, EtherCAT — they add real-time data exchange for I/O and motion.
  • Advantages: high speed and bandwidth, large networks, one network from field to enterprise, standard low-cost components, web/remote access and wireless extension. Limitations: needs real-time extensions for determinism and must be protected against cyber-attacks.

2023 · Q2(a)What is meant by data communication? Why does industrial automation require it? 06Topic: data communication

Data communication is the transfer of information (data) from one point to another through a transmission medium. It needs a transmitter, a receiver, a link (medium) between them and a protocol that both understand. In industrial automation it provides the interconnection between sensors, actuators, controllers and PCs; two or more devices connected for data exchange form a network.

Why industrial automation requires it:

  1. To carry measurements from field devices to controllers and commands from controllers to actuators.
  2. To coordinate several PLCs, drives and robots on one machine or line.
  3. To give HMI/SCADA operators real-time status, trends and alarms, including from remote sites.
  4. To reduce wiring: one network cable replaces many individual signal wires.
  5. To configure, calibrate and diagnose smart devices remotely.
  6. To send production data to MES/ERP for planning, quality and traceability.
Source lectureAsief Sir · Data Communication (Data Communication.pdf, p. 1)
2023 · Q2(b)Define the following terms: (i) Node (ii) Network media (iii) Protocol (iv) Bus topology and (v) Router 12Topic: network terms

(i) Node: any device connected to a network that can send, receive or forward data. In an industrial network a node can be a controller (PLC, PAC or DCS), a field device (sensor/transmitter or actuator), an HMI, a server or a workstation.

(ii) Network media: the physical or wireless channel that interconnects the nodes and carries the signals. Wired media: copper twisted-pair cables (CAT5/CAT6), copper coaxial cables (RG59) and fibre-optic cables. Wireless media: radio waves — Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, cellular.

(iii) Protocol: the set of rules (the agreed structure) by which devices communicate — how data are encoded, framed, addressed, timed, checked for errors and acknowledged — so that the receiver can understand what the transmitter sends. Examples: PROFIBUS, PROFINET, Modbus, HART, TCP/IP.

(iv) Bus topology: a network layout in which every node is connected to a single cable segment called the trunk, backbone or bus, with termination resistors at both ends to improve signal quality (Fig. 3.1(b)). Data sent by one node travel to all nodes, but only the addressed node accepts them (like a teacher calling one student by name). Example: PLCs, HMIs and remote I/O on PROFIBUS. It is cheap and easy to extend, but a break in the trunk affects the network.

(v) Router: a network device that connects multiple switches and their networks to form a larger network and forwards packets between networks using IP addresses (OSI layer 3). It lets devices networked by a switch reach other networks or the internet, and chooses the best path for each packet.

Source lectureAsief Sir · Data Communication (Data Communication.pdf, pp. 1–2); Data Communication (Data Communication.pdf, p. 9)
2023 · Q2(c)Briefly explain PROFIBUS and PROFINET. Relatively compare them. 14Topic: PROFIBUS vs PROFINET

PROFIBUS (Process Field Bus) is a serial fieldbus standard (IEC 61158) for connecting PLCs to distributed field devices (Fig. 3.2). PROFIBUS DP connects controllers with remote I/O, drives and valve islands at up to 12 Mbit/s over RS-485 shielded twisted pair in a line (bus) topology with terminators; PROFIBUS PA connects process instruments at 31.25 kbit/s with power over the bus and intrinsic safety. Access is by token passing among masters and master–slave polling of slaves; up to 126 addresses (32 stations per segment); devices are integrated with GSD files.

PROFINET (Process Field Net) is the open industrial Ethernet standard of the same organisation (PI), Ethernet-based successor of PROFIBUS (Fig. 3.3). A PROFINET IO system has an IO controller (PLC), IO devices (remote I/O, drives, robots) and an IO supervisor (HMI/engineering PC). It runs at 100 Mbit/s full duplex on switched Ethernet with star, line, tree or ring topology. It offers three performance classes: TCP/IP for configuration and diagnostics, RT for cyclic I/O (≈ 1–10 ms) and IRT for motion control (≤ 1 ms, jitter < 1 µs). Devices are named and addressed by IP/MAC and described by GSDML files; PROFIBUS segments connect via proxies.

Relative comparison:

FeaturePROFIBUS (DP)PROFINET (IO)
TechnologySerial fieldbus, RS-485Industrial Ethernet
Transmission rateUp to 12 Mbit/s, half duplex100 Mbit/s – 1 Gbit/s, full duplex
Bus accessToken passing + master/slaveProvider/consumer, switched
Max. devices126 (32 per segment)Practically unlimited
User data per telegram244 bytes1440 bytes
TopologyLine, needs terminationStar, line, tree, ring (redundant)
AddressingStation address (0–125)Device name, IP and MAC
Cable / connectorViolet 2-wire cable, 9-pin D-subCAT5e/6, RJ45/M12, fibre
Real-timeDeterministic, cycle grows with slavesRT and IRT (≤ 1 ms, isochronous)
IT integration, wirelessNo / noYes (TCP/IP, web) / yes (WLAN)
DiagnosticsBasicExtensive, topology detection
Typical useExisting plants, process instruments (PA)New plants, motion control, Industry 4.0

In short, PROFINET is faster, larger, more flexible and IT-friendly, while PROFIBUS remains simple, proven and dominant in installed (especially process) plants; both share the same device model and can coexist through proxies.

2024 · Q4(a)Why is data communication necessary in process industries? 04Topic: need for data communication

Process plants (refineries, chemical, power, water, food) are large and run continuously with thousands of instruments spread over a wide area. Data communication is necessary to:

  1. bring field measurements (temperature, pressure, flow, level, composition) to the controllers and send controller outputs to valves and pumps in real time;
  2. let operators in a central control room monitor and supervise the whole plant (DCS/SCADA), receive alarms and change set points;
  3. coordinate interacting units and safety interlocks across the plant;
  4. configure, calibrate and diagnose smart transmitters remotely (HART, fieldbus) — essential in hazardous or hard-to-reach areas;
  5. reduce field wiring and installation cost;
  6. record historical data for quality, optimisation, regulatory reports and integration with MES/ERP.
