2024 · Q4(c)Briefly describe HART protocol with proper sketch. 10Topic: HART protocol

HART (Highway Addressable Remote Transducer) is an open hybrid communication protocol that superimposes a digital signal on the standard 4–20 mA analog current loop, so that analog and digital information travel simultaneously on the same pair of wires.

Sketch:

Working:

  1. The transmitter controls the loop current between 4 and 20 mA in proportion to the measured variable; this analog signal is used for control as usual.
  2. Digital data are sent by frequency-shift keying (Bell 202): a 1200 Hz sine wave represents logic 1 and 2200 Hz represents logic 0, with amplitude ±0.5 mA, at 1200 bit/s.
  3. Because the sine wave has zero average value, it does not change the DC (analog) reading; the analog receiver filters it out, while the HART modem decodes it.
  4. HART is master–slave: the field device answers commands from a primary master (DCS/PLC HART card) or a secondary master (hand-held communicator, laptop). In burst mode the device can transmit continuously.
  5. At least 250 Ω loop resistance is needed to develop a readable FSK voltage.

Modes: point-to-point (analog + digital) and multidrop (up to 15/63 devices, current fixed at 4 mA, digital only). Digital data: extra process variables, tag, range, calibration, status and diagnostics. Advantages: existing wiring, remote configuration and diagnostics. Limitation: slow (1200 bit/s); WirelessHART extends it to a 2.4 GHz mesh.

Source lectureAsief Sir · Process Field Instrumentation (Process Field Instrumentations_Ver 1.2.pdf, p. 70); Seborg et al. – Process Dynamics and Control (reference text) (process-dynamics-and-control-dale-e.-seborg-thomas-f.-edgar-etc.-z-lib.org_.pdf, p. 484) — HART is only named on the slide; FSK details and sketch — see §3.7

4. SCADA and DCS ★★★

The syllabus item “Overview of SCADA and DCS systems” is asked in two of the three papers with high marks (35 marks in 2022, 15 in 2024), but none of the lecture files covers it. This chapter is therefore written from standard references (Seborg et al., Process Dynamics and Control, Appendix A, which is in the course folder; Bailey & Wright, Practical SCADA for Industry; Boyer, SCADA).

4.1 What Is SCADA?

Definition
SCADA (Supervisory Control And Data Acquisition) is a computer-based system that gathers data from remote equipment spread over a large geographical area, presents it to operators at a central station, and lets them exercise supervisory control (start/stop, open/close, change set points) over long-distance communication links. The real-time control loops run locally in RTUs/PLCs at the remote sites; the central SCADA system supervises them.

4.2 Hardware of a Simple SCADA System

HardwareFunction
Field instrumentsSensors and transmitters (level, pressure, flow, voltage, current, temperature), switches, and actuators (pumps, motorised valves, breakers) at the remote site.
Remote terminal unit (RTU)Rugged microprocessor unit at the remote site: reads analog and digital inputs, drives outputs, time-stamps events, stores data and communicates with the master over long links (often with battery/solar backup).
PLC / IEDPLCs are often used instead of RTUs because they also run local control logic; intelligent electronic devices (protection relays, meters) in substations.
Communication systemModems, licensed radio, microwave, fibre-optic links, cellular (GSM/4G) routers, satellite, leased lines, Ethernet WAN, with protocols such as Modbus, DNP3, IEC 60870-5-101/104.
Master terminal unit (MTU) / SCADA serverCentral computer (usually duplicated, hot standby) that polls the RTUs, processes data, checks alarms, issues commands and serves the HMIs.
HMI / operator workstationsComputers with large displays showing mimic diagrams, alarms, trends; operators issue commands here.
Historian / database serverStores time-stamped process data for trends, reports and analysis.
Engineering workstationUsed to configure the SCADA database, displays and RTU/PLC programs.
AuxiliariesLAN switches, firewalls, printers/alarm loggers, GPS time server, UPS power supplies, video wall.

4.3 Master-to-Remote Data Transfer

  • Polling (master–slave, request–response): the master interrogates every RTU in turn with a message containing the RTU address, function code and a checksum (CRC). The addressed RTU replies with its current analog values, digital states and alarms; the others ignore the message. When the last RTU has been polled the cycle repeats (scan cycle of seconds to minutes). If no reply arrives within a time-out the master retries and then flags a communication failure.
  • Report by exception: to save bandwidth the RTU sends only values that have changed by more than a dead-band, plus a periodic integrity poll of all data.
  • Unsolicited reporting: on capable links (DNP3, IEC 104) the RTU can send urgent alarms immediately without waiting to be polled.
  • Control commands: the master sends commands or set points to an RTU, often with select-before-operate (select → check-back → execute) for safety; the RTU acknowledges execution.
  • Other functions: time synchronisation of RTU clocks, download of configuration, error checking and retransmission.

4.4 Features and Capabilities of a Modern SCADA System

  • Real-time data acquisition from thousands of tags over wide areas.
  • Graphical HMI with mimic diagrams, faceplates and navigation; web and mobile clients.
  • Alarm and event management: prioritisation, time-stamping (to milliseconds), acknowledgement, SMS/e-mail notification.
  • Trending and historian: long-term storage, historical and real-time trends.
  • Supervisory control: remote start/stop, open/close, set-point changes, scheduling, recipe download.
  • Reporting and analytics: production, energy and regulatory reports; KPIs, dashboards.
  • Redundancy: hot-standby servers, redundant networks and communication paths.
  • Open connectivity: OPC UA, Modbus, DNP3, IEC 60870-5-104, MQTT; integration with MES/ERP, GIS and cloud.
  • Security: user authentication and roles, audit trail, encryption, firewalls.
  • Scalability and distributed architecture; scripting and calculation engines.

4.5 Advantages of SCADA over Manual Control

AspectTraditional manual controlSCADA
MonitoringOperators visit sites and read local gaugesAll sites monitored continuously from one control room
Response timeFaults found late (next visit or complaint)Instant alarms; fast remote action
Manpower and travelMany operators, vehicles, travel costFew operators; less travel
DataHand-written log sheets, errors, gapsAccurate, time-stamped, automatically archived
Decision makingBased on partial, delayed informationTrends, reports and analytics for optimisation
SafetyStaff exposed at hazardous sitesRemote operation; fewer site visits
EfficiencyOver/under-pumping, energy waste, leaks unnoticedOptimised operation, leak and loss detection
ConsistencyDepends on individual operatorStandard procedures, automatic sequences

4.6 Distributed Control System (DCS)

Definition
A distributed control system (DCS) is a plant-wide control system in which the control functions are distributed among many controllers located near the process units, all connected by a high-speed, usually redundant, communication network (data highway) to operator stations, engineering workstations and application servers. It is designed for continuous and batch process control at a single site, with thousands of closely interacting PID loops and a common database and operator interface.

Components of a DCS (Seborg et al., App. A.3.4): (1) a redundant control network (data highway); (2) workstations; (3) real-time clocks; (4) operator stations with colour graphics; (5) engineering workstations for configuration; (6) remote control units (controllers with I/O, often with multiplexers) that execute PID, logic and sequences close to the process; (7) application stations (databases, optimisation, OPC); (8) mass storage and historian; (9) fieldbuses and smart devices.

4.7 DCS versus SCADA

AspectDCSSCADA
Main purposeProcess-oriented: closed-loop control of a continuous/batch processData-acquisition-oriented: supervision of geographically dispersed equipment
Geographical areaOne plant site (compact)Large areas: tens to thousands of km
Where control is doneControllers of the DCS itself, tightly integratedLocally in RTUs/PLCs; central system supervises
CommunicationFast, reliable, redundant LAN; always connectedWAN links (radio, cellular, satellite) that may be slow or unreliable
Data handlingContinuous scanning; state of process always knownEvent-driven / polling; must handle lost links and stale data
Loop count, speedThousands of interacting PID loops, fast regulatory controlMostly monitoring and on/off supervisory commands
EngineeringSingle integrated database, vendor-specific systemOpen, multi-vendor RTUs/PLCs and protocols
Operator focusProcess trends, loop faceplatesAlarms, events, site status
Typical industries / examplesOil refinery, fertiliser and chemical plants, power-station boiler and turbine control, cement and paper millsElectricity transmission grid (substations to a load-dispatch centre), water supply and sewage networks, oil and gas pipelines, railways, irrigation

The boundary is becoming blurred: modern DCSs support remote sites, and modern SCADA systems with PLCs perform substantial control; but the distinction above is the one expected in the exam.

4.8 Solved Past Questions

2022 · Q3(a)What is DCS? How does DCS differ from SCADA system? Support your answer with appropriate example. 12Topic: DCS vs SCADA

DCS (distributed control system) is a plant-wide process control system in which control is distributed over many controllers placed close to the process units, connected by a redundant high-speed network to operator stations, engineering workstations and historians (Fig. 4.3). Each controller runs PID loops, logic and sequences for its unit; operators supervise the whole plant from a common interface and database. DCS is used for continuous and batch processes where many loops interact.

Differences between DCS and SCADA:

BasisDCSSCADA
OrientationProcess-oriented (control)Event/data-oriented (supervision and data acquisition)
Area coveredSingle plantWide geographical area
Control locationIntegrated DCS controllers execute closed-loop controlLocal RTUs/PLCs; central station gives supervisory commands
CommunicationHigh-speed redundant LAN, always availableLong-distance, lower-bandwidth links (radio, cellular, satellite), may fail
Data acquisitionContinuous scanning of all pointsPolling / report by exception
LoopsThousands of fast, interacting loopsMainly monitoring, alarms, on/off control
SystemSingle vendor, integrated databaseMulti-vendor, open protocols

Examples. DCS: an oil refinery or a urea-fertiliser plant — hundreds of temperature, pressure, flow and level loops in distillation columns and reactors are controlled by DCS controllers in the plant and supervised from the central control room. SCADA: a city water-supply network — pumping stations and reservoirs many kilometres apart each have an RTU/PLC that runs the pumps locally; the central SCADA polls them by radio or cellular link, shows levels and flows, raises alarms and lets the operator start pumps remotely. Similarly, the national electricity grid is supervised by SCADA from a load-dispatch centre.

Source lectureAsief Sir · Seborg et al. – Process Dynamics and Control (reference text) (process-dynamics-and-control-dale-e.-seborg-thomas-f.-edgar-etc.-z-lib.org_.pdf, pp. 481–482) — DCS only, from the reference text; SCADA and the comparison are not in the lecture files — see §4.6–4.7
2022 · Q3(b)Briefly explain master to remote data transfer in SCADA system. 08Topic: SCADA communication

In SCADA the central master station (MTU) exchanges data with the remote terminal units (RTUs) over a WAN, normally on a master–slave (polling) basis (Fig. 4.2):

  1. Polling cycle: the master sends a request to RTU 1 containing the RTU address, a function code (e.g. read analog inputs) and a CRC checksum. Only the addressed RTU answers.
  2. Response: the RTU returns the requested data — analog values, digital statuses, counters, alarm flags with time stamps — with its own checksum. The master checks the CRC, updates its database and HMI, and moves on to RTU 2, RTU 3 … then repeats the cycle.
  3. Time-outs and retries: if an RTU does not reply within a set time the master retries a few times and then raises a communication-failure alarm.
  4. Report by exception: to save bandwidth, RTUs may send only the values that changed beyond a dead-band, with periodic full (integrity) polls.
  5. Unsolicited messages: with protocols such as DNP3 or IEC 60870-5-104, an RTU can send urgent alarms immediately without waiting to be polled.
  6. Commands from master to remote: start/stop, open/close or new set points are sent to the RTU, often by select-before-operate; the RTU executes and returns an acknowledgement.
  7. Housekeeping: time synchronisation of RTU clocks and download of configuration.

Common protocols: Modbus RTU/TCP, DNP3, IEC 60870-5-101/104; media: radio, microwave, fibre, leased line, cellular, satellite.

Source lectureNot in the slides — answer built from standard theory (see §4.3 of this book)
2022 · Q3(c)What are the key features and capabilities of a modern SCADA system. 07Topic: SCADA features
  1. Real-time data acquisition from thousands of points at remote sites via RTUs, PLCs and IEDs.
  2. Graphical HMI — mimic diagrams, faceplates, web and mobile access.
  3. Alarm and event management — priorities, millisecond time-stamping, acknowledgement, SMS/e-mail notification.
  4. Historian and trending — long-term storage and real-time/historical trends.
  5. Supervisory control — remote commands, set-point changes, scheduling, recipes.
  6. Reports and analytics — production, energy, KPI dashboards, regulatory reports.
  7. Redundancy and reliability — hot-standby servers and redundant communication paths.
  8. Open connectivity and integration — OPC UA, Modbus, DNP3, IEC 104, MQTT; links to MES/ERP, GIS and cloud.
  9. Cybersecurity — role-based access, audit trails, encryption, firewalls.
  10. Scalability — add sites and tags without redesign.
Source lectureNot in the slides — answer built from standard theory (see §4.4 of this book)
2022 · Q3(d)What are the advantages of using a SCADA system compared to traditional manual control methods? 08Topic: SCADA advantages

(Printed as a second “3(c)” on the paper.)

  1. Centralised monitoring of widely dispersed sites from one control room, instead of staff travelling to read gauges.
  2. Fast response: faults and abnormal conditions raise alarms immediately and can be corrected remotely, reducing downtime and damage.
  3. Reduced manpower and operating cost: fewer operators, less travel and fuel.
  4. Accurate data: automatic, time-stamped logging replaces error-prone manual log sheets; full history available.
  5. Better decisions and optimisation: trends, reports and analytics show losses, leaks and energy waste.
  6. Improved safety: hazardous or remote sites are operated without people present.
  7. Consistency and reliability: standard automatic sequences, interlocks and redundancy do not depend on individual operators.
  8. Regulatory compliance and traceability: automatic reports and audit trails.

Compared with manual methods SCADA therefore gives a faster, safer, cheaper and better-documented operation (see the table in §4.5).

Source lectureNot in the slides — answer built from standard theory (see §4.5 of this book)
2024 · Q4(d)What is SCADA? Briefly describe the hardware commonly used in a simple SCADA system. 15Topic: SCADA hardware

SCADA (Supervisory Control And Data Acquisition) is a computer-based system that collects data from remote equipment spread over a large area, displays it to operators at a central control station, stores it and allows supervisory control (start/stop, open/close, set-point changes) over long-distance communication links. The fast local control is done by RTUs/PLCs at the sites; SCADA supervises them. Typical applications: power transmission and distribution, water supply, oil and gas pipelines, railways.

Hardware of a simple SCADA system (Fig. 4.1):

  1. Field instruments and actuators — sensors/transmitters for level, pressure, flow, temperature, voltage, current; limit switches; actuators such as pump starters, motorised valves and circuit breakers. They produce the raw signals (4–20 mA, 24 V on/off) and carry out commands.
  2. Remote terminal units (RTUs) — rugged microprocessor-based units at each remote site with analog/digital input and output modules, a CPU, memory, real-time clock, communication port/modem and battery backup. They acquire and time-stamp field data, store it, execute commands and communicate with the master.
  3. Programmable logic controllers (PLCs) and IEDs — used in place of or beside RTUs where local control logic is needed (pump sequencing, interlocks); IEDs such as protection relays and smart meters in substations.
  4. Communication equipment — modems, licensed UHF/VHF radios, microwave, fibre-optic links, cellular (GSM/4G) routers, satellite terminals, Ethernet switches and routers, with protocols such as Modbus, DNP3 or IEC 60870-5-104.
  5. Master terminal unit (MTU) / SCADA server — the central computer (normally a redundant pair) that polls the RTUs, processes and stores the data, checks alarm limits and sends operator commands to the field.
  6. HMI / operator workstations — PCs with large monitors (or a video wall) displaying mimic diagrams, alarms, trends and reports, through which operators supervise and control the process.
  7. Historian / database server — stores time-stamped data for trends, reports and analysis.
  8. Engineering workstation — for configuring the database, graphics and RTU/PLC programs.
  9. Supporting hardware — LAN switches and firewalls, alarm printers, GPS time server, UPS and power supplies.
Source lectureNot in the slides — answer built from standard theory (see §4.1–4.2 of this book)

5. Process Field Instrumentation ★★★

This chapter follows the lecture Process Field Instrumentations (Ver 1.2): measurement terms, standard instrumentation signals and transmitter calibration, sensors for temperature, level, pressure and flow, final control elements, and ISA symbology. It carries the largest share of Section A marks in 2023 and 2024.

5.1 Sensor, Transducer, Transmitter and Instrument

TermDefinition (lecture)Output / example
SensorA device that detects a change in a physical stimulus by producing a physical response that is related to the value of the process variable.Raw physical or electrical response — e.g. resistance of an RTD, mV of a thermocouple, deflection of a diaphragm
TransducerA device that converts an instrumentation signal from one form (of energy) to another.Usually an electrical signal proportional to the measurand — e.g. strain gauge converts strain to ΔR; I/P converter converts mA to psi
TransmitterConverts and conditions the sensor/transducer output into a standardised signal compatible with the controller input and drives the transmission line. It performs two functions: signal generation and line driving.Standard signal: 4–20 mA, 1–5 V, 3–15 psig or digital (HART, fieldbus)
InstrumentA device that senses a physical quantity (the measurand) and transforms it into a readable or usable output for indication, recording, transmission or control.Thermometer: temperature → visual reading

5.2 Standard Instrumentation Signal Levels

  • Pneumatic: 3–15 psig (≈ 20–100 kPa). Before 1960 the process industries used air-pressure signals almost exclusively, generated by mechanical force-balance elements.
  • Electronic current: 4–20 mA DC — the most common transmitter output since about 1960. (Older systems used 10–50 mA; 0–20 mA is also met.)
  • Electronic voltage: 1–5 V DC (also 0–10 V, 0–5 V) — suited only to short distances, e.g. inside a control panel.
  • Digital: HART (digital over 4–20 mA), BRAIN, FOUNDATION Fieldbus, PROFIBUS PA, and wireless (ISA100, WirelessHART).

Transmitters are normally direct-acting (output rises when the measured variable rises); reverse-acting ones (Km<0K_m<0Km​<0) are sometimes used, e.g. for level. Most transmitters have an adjustable input range (span).

Why current (4–20 mA) for long-distance transmission
  1. A current loop delivers the same current at every point of a series loop, so the signal is not affected by wire and connector resistance, which change with wire length, temperature and ageing; a voltage signal is attenuated by these resistances (lecture).
  2. Live zero: 4 mA = 0 % of range, so 0 mA means a broken wire or failed transmitter — faults are detectable; the 4 mA also powers 2-wire transmitters over the same pair.
  3. Noise immunity: the low-impedance current loop picks up little electrical noise compared with a high-impedance voltage input.
  4. Several receivers (indicator, recorder, controller) can be connected in series, and a 250 Ω resistor converts 4–20 mA into 1–5 V where a voltage is needed.

5.2.1 Linear transmitter: zero, span and gain

Transmitter calibration equation (lecture)
ym=Km (y−y0)+ym0,Km=output rangetransmitter span=ym2−ym1y2−y1y_m=K_m\,(y-y_0)+y_{m0},\qquad K_m=\frac{\text{output range}}{\text{transmitter span}}=\frac{y_{m2}-y_{m1}}{y_2-y_1}ym​=Km​(y−y0​)+ym0​,Km​=transmitter spanoutput range​=y2​−y1​ym2​−ym1​​ yyy = measured variable, y0y_0y0​ = lower range value (zero), span = upper − lower range value, ymy_mym​ = output signal, ym0y_{m0}ym0​ = output at the zero (4 mA). Equivalent form: O−Omin⁡=Omax⁡−Omin⁡Imax⁡−Imin⁡ (I−Imin⁡)O-O_{\min}=\dfrac{O_{\max}-O_{\min}}{I_{\max}-I_{\min}}\,(I-I_{\min})O−Omin​=Imax​−Imin​Omax​−Omin​​(I−Imin​).

Lecture example: a temperature transmitter with an RTD is ranged 50–150 °C → 4–20 mA. Zero = 50 °C, span = 100 °C, Km=20−4150−50=0.16K_m=\dfrac{20-4}{150-50}=0.16Km​=150−5020−4​=0.16 mA/°C, so Tm=0.16(T−50)+4T_m=0.16(T-50)+4Tm​=0.16(T−50)+4 mA.

5.2.2 Characteristics of a measurement system (short)

Accuracy — closeness of the reading to the true value (often % of full scale). Precision — ability to reproduce a reading; accuracy can be improved by calibration only up to the precision. Static error — measured − true value. Resolution — smallest change detected. Sensitivity — output change per unit input change (e.g. 1 mV/°C); the range should not greatly exceed the values to be measured. Calibration — comparison with a primary standard, a more accurate secondary standard or a known input.

5.2.3 Selection of a sensor/transmitter

(1) the process variable; (2) measurement range — the required range must lie entirely within the instrument's range; (3) performance — accuracy, repeatability, speed; (4) reliability — little drift; (5) materials of construction; (6) availability and total cost; (7) installation requirements (invasive probes can foul).

5.3 Common Process Variables and Their Sensors

VariableCommon sensors (lecture tables)Principle (one line)
TemperatureRTD (Pt-100), thermocouple, thermistor, bimetallic thermometer, filled-system thermometer, radiation pyrometerRTD: resistance rises with T; thermocouple: Seebeck emf of two dissimilar metals ∝ ΔT
PressureBourdon tube, diaphragm/capsule/bellows, strain-gauge (piezoresistive), capacitive, piezoelectric, liquid columnElastic element deforms under pressure; deformation read mechanically or electrically
FlowOrifice, venturi, nozzle (differential pressure), turbine, ultrasonic, electromagnetic, Coriolis, vortex shedding, rotameterDP: Δp ∝ Q²; ultrasonic: transit-time difference ∝ velocity
LevelCapacitive probe, ultrasonic (time of flight), guided-wave radar (TDR), float, hydrostatic (DP), bubble tubeCapacitance changes with wetted length; echo time t = 2d/v
Physical propertiespH: glass electrode, ISFET; density: vibrating tube, Coriolis; humidity: capacitive; vibration: piezoelectric accelerometer—

5.3.1 Temperature

RTD: resistance of a metal rises with temperature, R=R0(1+α1T+α2T2+… )R=R_0(1+\alpha_1T+\alpha_2T^2+\dots)R=R0​(1+α1​T+α2​T2+…); platinum is preferred (high-temperature capability, long-term stability, noble metal, nearly linear). Pt-100 = 100 Ω at 0 °C; Callendar–Van Dusen equation with A=3.9083×10−3A=3.9083\times10^{-3}A=3.9083×10−3, B=−5.775×10−7B=-5.775\times10^{-7}B=−5.775×10−7. Thermocouple: two dissimilar metals joined at the measuring junction produce an emf E=aΔθ+bΔθ2≈aΔθE=a\Delta\theta+b\Delta\theta^2\approx a\Delta\thetaE=aΔθ+bΔθ2≈aΔθ (Seebeck effect); needs extension wire of the same material and cold-junction compensation. Types J, K, T, E, N, R, S, B. RTD: more accurate, stable and linear, needs excitation, slower; thermocouple: self-powered, rugged, cheap, wide range, non-linear, low voltage.

5.3.2 Pressure

Absolute pressure is measured from vacuum, gauge pressure from atmosphere (Pabs=Pgauge+PatmP_{abs}=P_{gauge}+P_{atm}Pabs​=Pgauge​+Patm​), differential pressure between two points. 1 bar = 10⁵ Pa = 14.5 psi. Sensing elements: flat/corrugated diaphragms, capsules, bellows, Bourdon tubes (C, twisted, helical, spiral). Bourdon tube: a curved, flattened tube closed at one end tends to straighten under pressure and moves a pointer through a lever and rack-and-pinion. Strain-gauge sensor: gauges bonded to a diaphragm in a Wheatstone bridge; gauge factor GF=δR/Rδl/l=1+2ν+δρ/ρδl/lGF=\dfrac{\delta R/R}{\delta l/l}=1+2\nu+\dfrac{\delta\rho/\rho}{\delta l/l}GF=δl/lδR/R​=1+2ν+δl/lδρ/ρ​. Capacitive sensor: the diaphragm is one capacitor plate; pressure changes the gap and the capacitance (differential design doubles the signal).

5.3.3 Level

Capacitive: a rod electrode and the tank wall form a capacitor (C=εA/dC=\varepsilon A/dC=εA/d); as the level rises, more of the probe is surrounded by liquid of different permittivity, so CCC rises and the transmitter outputs 4–20 mA. Ultrasonic time of flight: a piezoelectric transducer on top sends a pulse that reflects from the surface; t=2d/vt=2d/vt=2d/v gives distance ddd and level L=h−dL=h-dL=h−d (sound ≈ 340 m/s in air, depends on temperature). Guided-wave radar (TDR): microwave pulse travels down a probe and reflects at the surface; unaffected by dust, vapour, pressure and temperature; can detect interfaces.

5.4 Flow Measurement

5.4.1 Differential-pressure (obstruction) flowmeters

An orifice plate, venturi tube or flow nozzle restricts the pipe; the fluid speeds up in the restriction and its static pressure falls. With continuity A1u1=A2u2A_1u_1=A_2u_2A1​u1​=A2​u2​ and Bernoulli for incompressible, frictionless flow p1+12ρu12=p2+12ρu22p_1+\tfrac12\rho u_1^2=p_2+\tfrac12\rho u_2^2p1​+21​ρu12​=p2​+21​ρu22​:

u2=11−(A2/A1)22(p1−p2)ρ,Q=C A2 11−β42 Δpρ(β=d/D)u_2=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(A_2/A_1)^2}}\sqrt{\frac{2(p_1-p_2)}{\rho}},\qquad Q=C\,A_2\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\beta^4}}\sqrt{\frac{2\,\Delta p}{\rho}}\quad(\beta=d/D)u2​=1−(A2​/A1​)2​1​ρ2(p1​−p2​)​​,Q=CA2​1−β4​1​ρ2Δp​​(β=d/D)

so Q∝ΔpQ\propto\sqrt{\Delta p}Q∝Δp​. Over 40 % of industrial flow measurements are still made this way: robust, no moving parts, suits turbulent flow — but poor accuracy at low flow, strict straight-pipe requirements, and a permanent pressure loss that must be paid for with pumping energy.

5.4.2 Ultrasonic flowmeters

Where flow must be measured without head loss or pressure drop — no moving parts, no restriction — two meters qualify: electromagnetic and ultrasonic. Ultrasonic meters work on nearly any liquid, and their cost is nearly independent of pipe diameter; electromagnetic meters need a minimum electrical conductivity and their price rises steeply with diameter.

Transit-time principle. The sound velocity ccc and the flow velocity add vectorially. Along a path of length LwL_wLw​ at angle φ\varphiφ to the pipe axis, the downstream (1 → 2) and upstream (2 → 1) transit times are

t12=Lwc+vˉacos⁡φ,t21=Lwc−vˉacos⁡φ.t_{12}=\frac{L_w}{c+\bar v_a\cos\varphi},\qquad t_{21}=\frac{L_w}{c-\bar v_a\cos\varphi}.t12​=c+vˉa​cosφLw​​,t21​=c−vˉa​cosφLw​​.

Taking reciprocals and subtracting removes ccc (which changes with temperature):

1t12−1t21=(c+vˉacos⁡φ)−(c−vˉacos⁡φ)Lw=2vˉacos⁡φLw⇒vˉa=Lw2cos⁡φ(1t12−1t21)=D2sin⁡φcos⁡φ(1t12−1t21)\begin{aligned}\frac1{t_{12}}-\frac1{t_{21}}&=\frac{(c+\bar v_a\cos\varphi)-(c-\bar v_a\cos\varphi)}{L_w}=\frac{2\bar v_a\cos\varphi}{L_w}\\ \Rightarrow\quad\bar v_a&=\frac{L_w}{2\cos\varphi}\left(\frac1{t_{12}}-\frac1{t_{21}}\right)=\frac{D}{2\sin\varphi\cos\varphi}\left(\frac1{t_{12}}-\frac1{t_{21}}\right)\end{aligned}t12​1​−t21​1​⇒vˉa​​=Lw​(c+vˉa​cosφ)−(c−vˉa​cosφ)​=Lw​2vˉa​cosφ​=2cosφLw​​(t12​1​−t21​1​)=2sinφcosφD​(t12​1​−t21​1​)​

using Lw=D/sin⁡φL_w=D/\sin\varphiLw​=D/sinφ. The path velocity is converted to the area-mean velocity vˉ\bar vvˉ (Gessner: vˉa=43vˉ\bar v_a=\tfrac43\bar vvˉa​=34​vˉ for laminar and 1.07 vˉ1.07\,\bar v1.07vˉ for turbulent flow) and Q=vˉ πD2/4Q=\bar v\,\pi D^2/4Q=vˉπD2/4. Transit-time meters need clean liquids or gases (water, oil).

Sign of the slide formula
Slide p. 67 writes vˉa=Lw2cos⁡φ(1t21−1t12)\bar v_a=\frac{L_w}{2\cos\varphi}\big(\frac1{t_{21}}-\frac1{t_{12}}\big)vˉa​=2cosφLw​​(t21​1​−t12​1​). With the slide's own definitions on p. 66 (t12t_{12}t12​ downstream, the shorter time) this is negative; the correct order is 1t12−1t21\frac1{t_{12}}-\frac1{t_{21}}t12​1​−t21​1​ as derived above (the magnitude is the same).

Doppler ultrasonic meter: ultrasound reflected by suspended particles or bubbles moving with the liquid returns with a frequency shift proportional to the flow velocity; needs at least about 100 ppm of 100 µm particles or bubbles — ideal for slurries and wastewater, not for clean liquids.

Electromagnetic meter: a conductive liquid moving through a magnetic field induces a voltage E=kBDvE=kBDvE=kBDv between electrodes (Faraday's law); no obstruction, but needs conductivity.

5.5 Transmitters and Final Control Elements

A transmitter is placed close to the sensor to shorten special wiring (e.g. thermocouple extension wire) and converts the sensor signal into 4–20 mA, a digital signal (HART, BRAIN, FOUNDATION Fieldbus) or a wireless signal (ISA100). 2-wire transmitters take power and send the signal on the same pair; 4-wire transmitters have separate power and signal pairs. Mounting styles: field-mount (dual-compartment housing), head-mount (“hockey puck”) and panel/DIN-rail mount.

The final control element (usually a control valve, or a pump/motor or heater) manipulates the process. A pneumatic control valve has a body, trim (plug), seat and a spring-diaphragm actuator: the controller signal (via an I/P converter, 3–15 psi) pushes the diaphragm against the spring. Air-to-open (fail-closed) or air-to-close (fail-open) is chosen for safety. Valve dynamics are approximated by Gv(s)=Kve−θs/(τvs+1)G_v(s)=K_v e^{-\theta s}/(\tau_v s+1)Gv​(s)=Kv​e−θs/(τv​s+1) with τv≪\tau_v\llτv​≪ process time constant; a valve positioner removes hysteresis, deadband and stick-slip.

The International Society of Automation (ISA S5.1) defines symbols for process and instrumentation diagrams (P&IDs). An instrument is shown by a balloon containing a tag: functional letters on top, loop number below.

Line → location: no line = field mounted; single line = front of the main panel (primary location, visible, accessible to operator); double line = front of a secondary/auxiliary panel (accessible); dotted line = rear of the main panel (not visible, not accessible).

Device symbols (lecture pp. 98–99): venturi tube, orifice plate, Coriolis, ultrasonic (sonic) flowmeter — square with an S-shaped wave, vortex, turbine flowmeters; gate and globe valves; spring-diaphragm actuator (dome on a stem), the same with a positioner (small box on the stem), motor-operated (circle with M), solenoid (square with S) and manual (T) actuators.

Lecture examples (p. 100): TY-178 (circle, field, 4–20 mA in, 3–15 psi out) = temperature-loop I/P converter in the field; FRC-97 (hexagon) = flow recording controller, a computer function, accessible; PRT-89 (diamond in square) = pressure recording transmitter, a PLC function in a secondary accessible location; LAH-222 (circle in square, dotted line) = level alarm high, not accessible.

5.7 Solved Past Questions

2023 · Q3(a)Define sensor, transducer, and transmitter. What are the different standard signal levels in industrial automation system? 10Topic: measurement terms · standard signals

Sensor: a device that detects a change in a physical stimulus (temperature, pressure, flow, level …) and produces a physical response related to the value of the process variable — e.g. an RTD whose resistance changes with temperature, a diaphragm that deflects with pressure.

Transducer: a device that converts a signal from one form of energy to another, usually into an electrical signal proportional to the measurand — e.g. a strain gauge (strain → resistance), a thermocouple (heat → mV), an I/P converter (current → air pressure).

Transmitter: a device that converts and conditions the sensor/transducer output into a standardised signal compatible with the controller input (e.g. 4–20 mA) and drives the transmission line to the controller; its two functions are signal generation and line driving. Example (Fig. 5.1): 0–100 psi → sensor/transducer 0–3 mV → transmitter 1–5 V → PLC analog input.

Standard signal levels:

TypeLevelRemarks
Pneumatic3–15 psig (20–100 kPa)Used almost exclusively before 1960; still used for valve actuators
Analog current4–20 mA DCMost common; live zero; best for long distances
Analog voltage1–5 V DC (0–10 V, 0–5 V)Short distances only (inside panels)
Digital / hybridHART, BRAIN, FOUNDATION Fieldbus, PROFIBUS PA, wireless (ISA100, WirelessHART)Multiple variables and diagnostics
Source lectureAsief Sir · Process Field Instrumentation (Process Field Instrumentations_Ver 1.2.pdf, pp. 9–13)

The four common process variables are temperature, pressure, flow and level; physical properties such as pH, density, composition and humidity are also measured.

2. Ultrasonic (time of flight)
3. Guided-wave radar, float, hydrostatic DP		Capacitance rises with wetted length; echo time t=2d/vt=2d/vt=2d/v, level L=h−dL=h-dL=h−d.
pH / densityGlass-electrode pH, ISFET; vibrating-tube densitometer, CoriolisElectrode potential ∝ pH; resonant frequency depends on density.

2023 · Q3(c)Suppose you are going to measure flow rate of a clear liquid flowing through a pipe of dia 40 cm. Without any flow rate reduction during measurement, which type of sensor will you suggest? Briefly explain its working procedure. 15Topic: ultrasonic transit-time flowmeter
Given Data
Clear (clean) liquid  |  pipe diameter D=40D=40D=40 cm =0.40=0.40=0.40 m (large pipe)  |  requirement: no flow reduction, i.e. no obstruction / pressure drop

Choice: a transit-time ultrasonic flowmeter (preferably clamp-on). Reasons:

  1. It has no moving parts and no restriction in the pipe, so there is no head loss and no flow reduction. Orifice, venturi and nozzle meters create a permanent pressure loss, and turbine meters obstruct the flow.
  2. The liquid is clear (clean): transit-time meters are ideal for clean liquids, whereas Doppler meters need suspended particles or bubbles.
  3. For a large 40 cm pipe, the cost of an ultrasonic meter is nearly independent of diameter, while an electromagnetic meter becomes very expensive (and needs a conductive liquid). Clamp-on transducers are mounted outside the pipe without cutting it or stopping the flow.

Working procedure (Fig. 5.2):

  1. Two piezoelectric transducers are mounted on opposite sides of the pipe so that the acoustic path of length LwL_wLw​ crosses the pipe at angle φ\varphiφ to its axis (Lw=D/sin⁡φL_w=D/\sin\varphiLw​=D/sinφ).
  2. Each transducer acts alternately as transmitter and receiver. A pulse sent downstream (sensor 1 → 2) is helped by the flow; a pulse sent upstream (2 → 1) is slowed: t12=Lwc+vˉacos⁡φ,t21=Lwc−vˉacos⁡φ.t_{12}=\frac{L_w}{c+\bar v_a\cos\varphi},\qquad t_{21}=\frac{L_w}{c-\bar v_a\cos\varphi}.t12​=c+vˉa​cosφLw​​,t21​=c−vˉa​cosφLw​​.
  3. The electronics measure both transit times very precisely and compute the mean axial velocity along the path (the sound speed ccc cancels): vˉa=Lw2cos⁡φ(1t12−1t21)=D2sin⁡φcos⁡φ(1t12−1t21).\bar v_a=\frac{L_w}{2\cos\varphi}\left(\frac1{t_{12}}-\frac1{t_{21}}\right)=\frac{D}{2\sin\varphi\cos\varphi}\left(\frac1{t_{12}}-\frac1{t_{21}}\right).vˉa​=2cosφLw​​(t12​1​−t21​1​)=2sinφcosφD​(t12​1​−t21​1​).
  4. The path velocity is corrected to the area-average velocity (turbulent flow: vˉ=vˉa/1.07\bar v=\bar v_a/1.07vˉ=vˉa​/1.07) and the volumetric flow rate is Q=vˉ⋅πD2/4Q=\bar v\cdot\pi D^2/4Q=vˉ⋅πD2/4.
  5. The transmitter outputs QQQ as 4–20 mA (or HART/fieldbus) and totalises volume.

Numerical illustration (assumed φ=45∘\varphi=45^\circφ=45∘, water c=1480c=1480c=1480 m/s, vˉa=1.5\bar v_a=1.5vˉa​=1.5 m/s):

Lw=0.40sin⁡45∘=0.5657 m,t12=381.946 μs,t21=382.494 μsL_w=\frac{0.40}{\sin45^\circ}=0.5657\ \text{m},\quad t_{12}=381.946\ \mu\text{s},\quad t_{21}=382.494\ \mu\text{s}Lw​=sin45∘0.40​=0.5657 m,t12​=381.946 μs,t21​=382.494 μs Δt=t21−t12≈0.548 μs,vˉ=1.51.07=1.402 m/s\Delta t=t_{21}-t_{12}\approx0.548\ \mu\text{s},\qquad \bar v=\frac{1.5}{1.07}=1.402\ \text{m/s}Δt=t21​−t12​≈0.548 μs,vˉ=1.071.5​=1.402 m/s Q=1.402×π(0.40)24=0.176 m3/s≈634 m3/hQ=1.402\times\frac{\pi(0.40)^2}{4}=0.176\ \text{m}^3/\text{s}\approx634\ \text{m}^3/\text{h}Q=1.402×4π(0.40)2​=0.176 m3/s≈634 m3/h
[INTUITION]The time difference is only about half a microsecond in 382 µs, so the electronics must resolve nanoseconds — modern meters do this digitally. Assumed values are for illustration; the question gives none.

Advantages: no pressure loss, no moving parts, bidirectional, wide range, low maintenance, clamp-on installation without process shutdown. Limitations: needs a clean liquid and a full pipe, a straight run of pipe upstream, and good acoustic coupling.

Source lectureAsief Sir · Process Field Instrumentation (Process Field Instrumentations_Ver 1.2.pdf, pp. 65–68)

2024 · Q3(b)List the standard instrumentation signals along with their corresponding levels. Which one is suitable for long-distance transmission and why? 07Topic: standard signals
Standard signalLevel
Pneumatic3–15 psig (20–100 kPa)
Analog current4–20 mA DC (older: 10–50 mA; also 0–20 mA)
Analog voltage1–5 V DC (also 0–5 V, 0–10 V)
DigitalHART (FSK ±0.5 mA on 4–20 mA), FOUNDATION Fieldbus, PROFIBUS PA, BRAIN, wireless

Suitable for long distance: the 4–20 mA current signal, because:

  1. in a series current loop the same current flows everywhere, so the signal is not affected by wire and connector resistance, which vary with length, temperature and ageing — a voltage signal would drop along the line;
  2. the low-impedance loop has high noise immunity;
  3. the live zero (4 mA) distinguishes a true zero reading from a broken wire (0 mA) and supplies power to 2-wire transmitters;
  4. several receivers can be connected in series and the signal converts easily to 1–5 V with a 250 Ω resistor.

Pneumatic signals are slow over long tubes, and voltage signals (1–5 V) are suitable only for short distances.

Source lectureAsief Sir · Process Field Instrumentation (Process Field Instrumentations_Ver 1.2.pdf, pp. 12–13)
2024 · Q3(c)Suppose the flow rate of a stream (acting as a disturbance variable) is required to measure for use in a feedforward controller. The stream contains clean liquid. Which flow measurement technique is suitable? Briefly explain it with a proper sketch. 14Topic: flow measurement for feedforward control

In feedforward control the disturbance is measured and the manipulated variable is changed before the controlled variable deviates. The flow measurement must therefore be accurate, fast and must not itself disturb the stream (no extra pressure drop that would change the flow).

Suitable technique: transit-time ultrasonic flow measurement. For a clean liquid it is accurate, has a fast electronic response, causes no pressure drop and no obstruction (so it does not alter the disturbance flow it measures), has no moving parts and can be clamped on without opening the line. (A Doppler meter would not work on a clean liquid; an orifice meter adds a permanent pressure loss and has a square-root, low-flow-inaccurate signal; a magnetic meter needs a conductive liquid.)

Explanation with sketch (Fig. 5.2):

  1. Two ultrasonic transducers are mounted on the pipe so that sound crosses it diagonally at angle φ\varphiφ over path length Lw=D/sin⁡φL_w=D/\sin\varphiLw​=D/sinφ.
  2. Pulses are sent alternately downstream and upstream. The flow speeds up the downstream pulse and slows the upstream one: t12=Lw/(c+vˉacos⁡φ)t_{12}=L_w/(c+\bar v_a\cos\varphi)t12​=Lw​/(c+vˉa​cosφ), t21=Lw/(c−vˉacos⁡φ)t_{21}=L_w/(c-\bar v_a\cos\varphi)t21​=Lw​/(c−vˉa​cosφ).
  3. The velocity is obtained from the difference of reciprocals, independent of the sound speed: vˉa=Lw2cos⁡φ(1t12−1t21)\bar v_a=\dfrac{L_w}{2\cos\varphi}\Big(\dfrac1{t_{12}}-\dfrac1{t_{21}}\Big)vˉa​=2cosφLw​​(t12​1​−t21​1​).
  4. Correcting to the area-mean velocity (vˉ=vˉa/1.07\bar v=\bar v_a/1.07vˉ=vˉa​/1.07 for turbulent flow) and multiplying by the pipe area gives Q=vˉ πD2/4Q=\bar v\,\pi D^2/4Q=vˉπD2/4.
  5. The transmitter sends QQQ (4–20 mA/HART) to the feedforward controller, which computes the required change of the manipulated variable.
Source lectureAsief Sir · Process Field Instrumentation (Process Field Instrumentations_Ver 1.2.pdf, pp. 65–68) — feedforward sketch not in the slides — see §5.7

6. Process Control: Feedback Loop, Modelling, Block Diagrams and PID Control ★★★

This chapter follows the hand-written lecture Process control v3 (pp. 2–23), the Modified PID controllers simulation slides and the class-test solution AJ CT2 solve. It covers the elements of a feedback loop, the dynamic model and block diagram of the stirred-tank blending process, P/PI/PID controllers, offset, kicks, reset windup and tuning. The derivations are written out in full because the 2023 and 2024 papers set 16- and 18-mark questions on them.

6.1 The Feedback Control Loop

ElementFunctionExample (stirred-tank heater)
Process (plant)The equipment whose output variable is to be controlled; disturbances act on it.Tank of liquid being heated
Sensor / transmitterMeasures the controlled variable and converts it to a standard signal ymy_mym​.Thermocouple + temperature transmitter
Comparator (summing junction)Forms the error e=ysp−yme=y_{sp}-y_me=ysp​−ym​; usually inside the controller.—
ControllerApplies the control law (on/off, P, PI, PID) to the error and computes the controller output ppp.Electronic PID controller / PLC
Final control element (actuator)Converts the controller output into a change of the manipulated variable.Electric heater (or steam control valve)
Set pointDesired value of the controlled variable (reference input).Desired liquid temperature

In the lecture's room-heating example, a thermostat compares room temperature with a band of 18–22 °C: below 18 °C the furnace and pump are switched on, above 22 °C off, and in between their state is left unchanged (on/off control with a dead band). The outside temperature is the disturbance. In the stirred-tank heating system, a thermocouple measures the liquid temperature as a millivolt signal, a transmitter converts it to a standard signal, the feedback controller computes the output, and the heater (final control element) adjusts the heat input.

Process-control variables
Controlled variable (CV) — the process output that is measured and kept at its set point (e.g. outlet composition xxx, tank level hhh, temperature TTT).
Manipulated variable (MV) — the process input that the controller adjusts through the final control element to keep the CV at its set point (e.g. flow w2w_2w2​ through the control valve).
Disturbance variable (DV) — a process input that affects the CV but is not adjusted by the controller (e.g. inlet composition x1x_1x1​, inlet flow q1q_1q1​, ambient temperature).
Set point (SP) — the desired value of the CV. Error e=ysp−yme=y_{sp}-y_me=ysp​−ym​.

6.2 Dynamic Model of the Continuous Stirred-Tank Blending Process

Two streams of a mixture of components A and B are blended in a perfectly mixed tank. Stream 1 has flow w1w_1w1​ (kg/min) and mass fraction of A x1x_1x1​; stream 2 is pure A (x2=1x_2=1x2​=1) with flow w2w_2w2​ set by a control valve; the outlet has flow www and composition xxx. Objective: control the outlet composition xxx. CV =x=x=x, MV =w2=w_2=w2​, disturbance =x1=x_1=x1​ (lecture p. 2).

Approximations (assumptions) used
(1) Perfect mixing — the outlet composition equals the tank composition xxx. (2) Constant density ρ\rhoρ. (3) Constant liquid volume VVV (overflow), so wˉ=wˉ1+wˉ2\bar w=\bar w_1+\bar w_2wˉ=wˉ1​+wˉ2​. (4) w1w_1w1​ is constant; stream 2 is pure A, x2=1x_2=1x2​=1. (5) The nonlinear model is linearised by a first-order Taylor series about the nominal steady state, and deviation variables are used. (6) The analyzer transmitter, I/P transducer and controller have negligible dynamics compared with the process (τ≫τm\tau\gg\tau_mτ≫τm​), so they are pure gains; the control valve is first order.

Step 1 — Mass and component balances

Rate of accumulation = rate in − rate out (+ rate produced, zero here, no reaction):

d(ρV)dt=w1+w2−w,d(ρVx)dt=w1x1+w2x2−wx.\frac{d(\rho V)}{dt}=w_1+w_2-w,\qquad \frac{d(\rho Vx)}{dt}=w_1x_1+w_2x_2-wx.dtd(ρV)​=w1​+w2​−w,dtd(ρVx)​=w1​x1​+w2​x2​−wx.

At steady state (bars): 0=wˉ1+wˉ2−wˉ0=\bar w_1+\bar w_2-\bar w0=wˉ1​+wˉ2​−wˉ and 0=wˉ1xˉ1+wˉ2xˉ2−wˉxˉ0=\bar w_1\bar x_1+\bar w_2\bar x_2-\bar w\bar x0=wˉ1​xˉ1​+wˉ2​xˉ2​−wˉxˉ.

Step 2 — Composition equation

With constant ρ\rhoρ: ρd(Vx)dt=ρxdVdt+ρVdxdt=(w1+w2−w)x+ρVdxdt\rho\frac{d(Vx)}{dt}=\rho x\frac{dV}{dt}+\rho V\frac{dx}{dt}=(w_1+w_2-w)x+\rho V\frac{dx}{dt}ρdtd(Vx)​=ρxdtdV​+ρVdtdx​=(w1​+w2​−w)x+ρVdtdx​. Substituting in the component balance:

w1x1+w2x2−wx=ρVdxdt+(w1+w2−w)x  ⇒  ρVdxdt=w1(x1−x)+w2(x2−x)≡f(x,x1,w2).w_1x_1+w_2x_2-wx=\rho V\frac{dx}{dt}+(w_1+w_2-w)x\;\Rightarrow\;\rho V\frac{dx}{dt}=w_1(x_1-x)+w_2(x_2-x)\equiv f(x,x_1,w_2).w1​x1​+w2​x2​−wx=ρVdtdx​+(w1​+w2​−w)x⇒ρVdtdx​=w1​(x1​−x)+w2​(x2​−x)≡f(x,x1​,w2​).

Step 3 — Linearisation

Expanding fff in a Taylor series about the steady state and truncating after the first-order terms (f(xˉ,xˉ1,wˉ2)=0f(\bar x,\bar x_1,\bar w_2)=0f(xˉ,xˉ1​,wˉ2​)=0):

ρVdxdt≈∂f∂x∣s(x−xˉ)+∂f∂x1∣s(x1−xˉ1)+∂f∂w2∣s(w2−wˉ2)\rho V\frac{dx}{dt}\approx\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right|_s(x-\bar x)+\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}\right|_s(x_1-\bar x_1)+\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial w_2}\right|_s(w_2-\bar w_2)ρVdtdx​≈∂x∂f​​s​(x−xˉ)+∂x1​∂f​​s​(x1​−xˉ1​)+∂w2​∂f​​s​(w2​−wˉ2​) ∂f∂x=−wˉ1−wˉ2=−wˉ,∂f∂x1=wˉ1,∂f∂w2=xˉ2−xˉ=1−xˉ.\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=-\bar w_1-\bar w_2=-\bar w,\qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}=\bar w_1,\qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial w_2}=\bar x_2-\bar x=1-\bar x.∂x∂f​=−wˉ1​−wˉ2​=−wˉ,∂x1​∂f​=wˉ1​,∂w2​∂f​=xˉ2​−xˉ=1−xˉ.

With deviation variables x′=x−xˉx'=x-\bar xx′=x−xˉ, x1′=x1−xˉ1x_1'=x_1-\bar x_1x1′​=x1​−xˉ1​, w2′=w2−wˉ2w_2'=w_2-\bar w_2w2′​=w2​−wˉ2​ (and dxdt=dx′dt\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{dx'}{dt}dtdx​=dtdx′​ because xˉ\bar xxˉ is constant):

ρVdx′dt=−wˉ x′+wˉ1 x1′+(1−xˉ) w2′.\rho V\frac{dx'}{dt}=-\bar w\,x'+\bar w_1\,x_1'+(1-\bar x)\,w_2'.ρVdtdx′​=−wˉx′+wˉ1​x1′​+(1−xˉ)w2′​.

Step 4 — Transfer functions

Laplace transform with zero initial conditions (deviation variables start at 0): ρVsX′(s)=−wˉX′(s)+wˉ1X1′(s)+(1−xˉ)W2′(s)\rho VsX'(s)=-\bar wX'(s)+\bar w_1X_1'(s)+(1-\bar x)W_2'(s)ρVsX′(s)=−wˉX′(s)+wˉ1​X1′​(s)+(1−xˉ)W2′​(s). Dividing by wˉ\bar wwˉ:

(ρVwˉs+1)X′(s)=wˉ1wˉX1′(s)+1−xˉwˉW2′(s)\Big(\frac{\rho V}{\bar w}s+1\Big)X'(s)=\frac{\bar w_1}{\bar w}X_1'(s)+\frac{1-\bar x}{\bar w}W_2'(s)(wˉρV​s+1)X′(s)=wˉwˉ1​​X1′​(s)+wˉ1−xˉ​W2′​(s)
Process model
X′(s)=K1τs+1X1′(s)+K2τs+1W2′(s),K1=wˉ1wˉ,K2=1−xˉwˉ,τ=ρVwˉ.X'(s)=\frac{K_1}{\tau s+1}X_1'(s)+\frac{K_2}{\tau s+1}W_2'(s),\qquad K_1=\frac{\bar w_1}{\bar w},\quad K_2=\frac{1-\bar x}{\bar w},\quad \tau=\frac{\rho V}{\bar w}.X′(s)=τs+1K1​​X1′​(s)+τs+1K2​​W2′​(s),K1​=wˉwˉ1​​,K2​=wˉ1−xˉ​,τ=wˉρV​.

6.3 Block Diagram of the Blending Control Loop

Each element of Fig. 6.2 is represented by a block with its transfer function and the units of its input and output (lecture pp. 8–10):

  1. Process: the model above; W2′W_2'W2′​ in kg/min, X′X'X′ and X1′X_1'X1′​ in mass fraction.
  2. Sensor/transmitter (AT): Xm′(s)/X′(s)=KmX_m'(s)/X'(s)=K_mXm′​(s)/X′(s)=Km​ [mA per mass fraction]. In general Km/(τms+1)K_m/(\tau_ms+1)Km​/(τm​s+1), but τ≫τm\tau\gg\tau_mτ≫τm​ (negligible dynamics) gives a pure gain.
  3. Controller (AC): P′(s)/E(s)=KcP'(s)/E(s)=K_cP′(s)/E(s)=Kc​ for proportional control, or Kc(1+1τIs)K_c\big(1+\frac1{\tau_Is}\big)Kc​(1+τI​s1​) for PI, with E=X~sp′−Xm′E=\tilde X_{sp}'-X_m'E=X~sp′​−Xm′​ [mA].
  4. I/P transducer (fast dynamics): Pt′(s)/P′(s)=KIPP_t'(s)/P'(s)=K_{IP}Pt′​(s)/P′(s)=KIP​ [psi/mA].
  5. Control valve (pneumatically actuated): W2′(s)/Pt′(s)=Kv/(τvs+1)W_2'(s)/P_t'(s)=K_v/(\tau_vs+1)W2′​(s)/Pt′​(s)=Kv​/(τv​s+1) [kg/min per psi].

Because the error is formed in mA, the set point (a mass fraction) is converted by the same gain as the transmitter: X~sp′=KmXsp′\tilde X_{sp}'=K_mX_{sp}'X~sp′​=Km​Xsp′​. Connecting the blocks gives the closed loop:

Closed-loop transfer functions (P control, Gc=KcG_c=K_cGc​=Kc​)

6.6 Problems with PID Control and Their Remedies

6.6.1 Proportional kick and derivative kick

A sudden (step) change in set point makes the error jump. The proportional term then jumps by KcΔyspK_c\Delta y_{sp}Kc​Δysp​ (proportional kick) and the derivative term, proportional to de/dtde/dtde/dt, becomes momentarily infinite (derivative kick, a spike limited only by the derivative filter). These spikes slam the valve, wear the actuator and upset the process. The way to handle them together is set-point weighting:

Set-point weighting (β–γ PID controller)
p′(t)=Kc[eP(t)+1τI∫0te(t) dt+τDdeD(t)dt]p'(t)=K_c\Big[e_P(t)+\frac1{\tau_I}\int_0^te(t)\,dt+\tau_D\frac{de_D(t)}{dt}\Big]p′(t)=Kc​[eP​(t)+τI​1​∫0t​e(t)dt+τD​dtdeD​(t)​] eP=βysp−y,e=ysp−y,eD=γysp−y,0≤β,γ≤1.e_P=\beta y_{sp}-y,\qquad e=y_{sp}-y,\qquad e_D=\gamma y_{sp}-y,\qquad 0\le\beta,\gamma\le1.eP​=βysp​−y,e=ysp​−y,eD​=γysp​−y,0≤β,γ≤1. β=γ=1\beta=\gamma=1β=γ=1: standard PID. γ=0\gamma=0γ=0: PI-D (derivative on measurement only — no derivative kick). β=γ=0\beta=\gamma=0β=γ=0: I-PD (only the integral acts on the error — no proportional or derivative kick). The integral term must always use the true error eee, otherwise offset would remain.

6.6.2 Reset (integral) windup

When a sustained error occurs — a large set-point change, start-up, or a disturbance beyond the range of the manipulated variable — the integral term keeps growing while the controller output is already saturated (valve fully open or shut). This extra build-up is reset windup. When the error finally changes sign the oversized integral term must first “unwind”, so the controlled variable overshoots badly and settles slowly. Anti-reset-windup (ARW) methods limit the integral term:

  • Clamping / conditional integration: freeze the integral while the output is saturated (equivalent to back-calculation).
  • Back-calculation (tracking): feed the difference between the saturated and the computed output back to the integrator to drive it toward the limit.
  • Integral limits: keep the integral term within set bounds (simple but sluggish).
  • PI with the integral implemented as a positive-feedback loop around the saturation (external reset; Seborg Fig. 8.8).

Tuning means choosing KcK_cKc​, τI\tau_IτI​, τD\tau_DτD​. Classical methods: Ziegler–Nichols continuous cycling, Ziegler–Nichols step (reaction-curve) method, Cohen–Coon, relay auto-tuning. Model-based methods: direct synthesis (DS) and internal model control (IMC).

2023 · Q4(c)Define controller variable and manipulated variable. 05Topic: controlled and manipulated variables

(“Controller variable” is read as controlled variable, the usual term.)

Controlled variable (CV): the process output variable that is measured and kept at a desired value (set point) by the control system. Example: in the blending process the outlet composition xxx is the controlled variable; in a level loop the tank level hhh.

Manipulated variable (MV): the process input variable that the controller adjusts, through the final control element, in order to keep the controlled variable at its set point. Example: the flow rate w2w_2w2​ of stream 2 adjusted by the control valve in the blending process; the inlet flow q2q_2q2​ in a level loop.

The controller output itself (signal ppp in mA) is sometimes called the controller variable; it sets the valve, which in turn changes the manipulated variable.

Source lectureAsief Sir · Process Control (hand-written lecture) (Process control v3.pdf, p. 2)
2024 · Q2(a)What are the components of the feedback control loop used in industrial automation? 05Topic: feedback loop components
  1. Process (plant): the equipment whose output (controlled variable) is regulated, e.g. a tank, heat exchanger or reactor; disturbances act on it.
  2. Sensor/transmitter: measures the controlled variable and sends a standard signal (4–20 mA) to the controller.
  3. Comparator: compares the measured value with the set point to give the error e=ysp−yme=y_{sp}-y_me=ysp​−ym​.
  4. Controller: applies the control law (on/off, P, PI, PID) to the error and generates the controller output.
  5. Final control element (actuator): usually a control valve (with I/P converter), pump or heater; it changes the manipulated variable.

Signals in the loop: set point, error, controller output, manipulated variable, disturbance, controlled variable and the feedback (measured) signal.

Source lectureAsief Sir · Process Field Instrumentation (Process Field Instrumentations_Ver 1.2.pdf, pp. 4–6)
2024 · Q2(b)What are the ways to eliminate proportional kick, derivative kick, and reset windup? Briefly describe any one of the methods. 12Topic: kicks and reset windup

Ways to eliminate:

ProblemCauseRemedies
Proportional kickStep change in set point makes KceK_ceKc​e jumpSet-point weighting with β<1\beta<1β<1; β=0\beta=0β=0 gives proportional action on the measurement only (I-PD); ramping or filtering the set point
Derivative kickde/dtde/dtde/dt is infinite at a set-point stepDerivative on measurement, −τD dym/dt-\tau_D\,dy_m/dt−τD​dym​/dt (γ=0\gamma=0γ=0, PI-D); derivative filter τDs/(ατDs+1)\tau_Ds/(\alpha\tau_Ds+1)τD​s/(ατD​s+1); set-point filtering
Reset windupIntegral keeps growing while the output is saturatedAnti-reset windup: clamping (conditional integration), back-calculation/tracking, integral limits, integral via positive-feedback loop (external reset)

Method described: set-point weighting. The controller uses different errors for the three modes:

p′(t)=Kc[eP(t)+1τI∫0te(t) dt+τDdeD(t)dt],eP=βysp−ym, e=ysp−ym, eD=γysp−ym,p'(t)=K_c\Big[e_P(t)+\frac1{\tau_I}\int_0^te(t)\,dt+\tau_D\frac{de_D(t)}{dt}\Big],\qquad e_P=\beta y_{sp}-y_m,\ e=y_{sp}-y_m,\ e_D=\gamma y_{sp}-y_m,p′(t)=Kc​[eP​(t)+τI​1​∫0t​e(t)dt+τD​dtdeD​(t)​],eP​=βysp​−ym​, e=ysp​−ym​, eD​=γysp​−ym​,

with 0≤β,γ≤10\le\beta,\gamma\le10≤β,γ≤1.

  • At a set-point step Δysp\Delta y_{sp}Δysp​, the proportional jump is only KcβΔyspK_c\beta\Delta y_{sp}Kc​βΔysp​ and the derivative spike is proportional to γ\gammaγ; with γ=0\gamma=0γ=0 the derivative acts on the measurement alone (PI-D) and the derivative kick disappears; with β=γ=0\beta=\gamma=0β=γ=0 only the integral acts on the error (I-PD, Fig. 6.5) and both kicks are removed.
  • The integral term keeps the full error eee, so there is still no offset.
  • For disturbances (set point constant) the response is identical to normal PID, because β,γ\beta,\gammaβ,γ only multiply yspy_{sp}ysp​.
  • The lecture's simulation (Fig. 6.6) shows the controller-output spike of about 116 for normal PID reduced to 58 with β=γ=0.5\beta=\gamma=0.5β=γ=0.5 and removed with β=γ=0\beta=\gamma=0β=γ=0; the PV then rises more smoothly (slower, with a smaller overshoot).

(For reset windup, the clamping method is shown in Fig. 6.7: freezing the integral while the output is saturated removes the large overshoot.)

7. PLC Questions Set in Section A (2022) ★★★

In the 2022 paper Section A also contained four PLC questions (2(c), 4(b), 4(c), 4(d)). PLCs are taught in Section B (Priyo Sir's lectures, e.g. 1.Automation.pptx, and W. Bolton, Programmable Logic Controllers), not in Asief Sir's slides, so this chapter gives the theory needed for these four questions in compact form.

7.1 What Is a PLC?

Definition
A programmable logic controller (PLC) is a rugged, microprocessor-based digital controller that uses a programmable memory to store instructions and to implement functions such as logic, sequencing, timing, counting and arithmetic, in order to control machines and processes through digital and analog inputs and outputs. It was introduced (1968–69) to replace hard-wired relay control panels; its main advantage is that it can be easily programmed and reprogrammed, and it is built to work reliably in industrial environments (noise, vibration, temperature, humidity).

Scan cycle. The CPU executes the program cyclically: (1) input scan — read all inputs into the input image table; (2) program scan — execute the user program rung by rung using the image values; (3) output scan — write the output image table to the output modules; plus housekeeping and communication. The time for one cycle is the scan time (typically a few ms).

7.2 Ladder Logic Essentials

A ladder diagram has two vertical power rails and horizontal rungs between them. Inputs appear as contacts: normally open ─| |─ (true when the input is ON) and normally closed ─|/|─ (true when OFF). Contacts in series form AND, contacts in parallel form OR, and the output coil ─( )─ is at the right. A contact of the output placed in parallel with a start condition is a latch (seal-in, holding) contact: once the output is ON it keeps itself ON until a series condition opens. To derive a ladder from a timing diagram: list each time interval with the input and output states, see whether the output is a pure Boolean function of the inputs (if the same input combination gives different outputs, memory — a latch — is needed), then write the logic and check it interval by interval.

2022 · Q2(c)What is meant by PLC? Draw a block diagram of a PLC showing the main functional components and explain the functions of each block. 12Topic: PLC hardware

PLC (programmable logic controller): a rugged, microprocessor-based digital controller that uses a programmable memory to store instructions implementing logic, sequencing, timing, counting and arithmetic functions, to control machines and processes through its inputs and outputs. It replaces hard-wired relay logic and can easily be reprogrammed when the control requirements change.

Functions of each block

  1. Power supply: converts the mains (120/230 V AC) into the low DC voltages needed by the processor (5 V) and the I/O modules (24 V DC); it is an integral part of the PLC.
  2. Input module (input interface): receives signals from field input devices — push buttons, limit and proximity switches, sensors — and converts them to the low-level logic signals used by the CPU. It provides optoisolation, filtering and signal conditioning; analog input modules convert 4–20 mA / 0–10 V signals to numbers with an ADC.
  3. CPU (processor): the “brain” of the PLC. It reads the input status, executes the user program (logic, timers, counters, arithmetic, data handling), makes the control decisions, updates the outputs, and handles communication and self-diagnostics in a repeated scan cycle (input scan → program scan → output scan).
  4. Memory: stores the operating system (ROM), the user program and the data — input/output image tables, timer and counter values, internal relays (RAM/EEPROM/flash).
  5. Output module (output interface): amplifies the CPU's logic-level output signals and switches the field output devices — relays, contactors, solenoid valves, lamps, motor starters — through relay, transistor (DC) or triac (AC) outputs, again with isolation; analog outputs use a DAC.
  6. Communications interface: exchanges data with HMIs, other PLCs, remote I/O, SCADA and networks (PROFIBUS, PROFINET, Modbus, Ethernet); handles device verification, data acquisition, synchronisation and connection management.
  7. Programming device: a PC with programming software (or a hand-held programmer) used to write, download, monitor and debug the program (ladder, FBD, IL, ST, SFC).
Source lectureNot in the slides of Asief Sir — PLC is a Section B topic (Priyo Sir, 1.Automation.pptx, slides 4–9); answer built from standard theory (see §7.1 of this book)
2022 · Q4(b)Draw the PLC Ladder circuit from the following output. 10Topic: ladder from a timing diagram

Step 1 — read the chart interval by interval.

Interval0–t1t1–t2t2–t3t3–t4t4–t5t5–t6after t6
I11001100
I21100110
Q1 (chart)1100110
(I1+Q1)⋅I2(I1+Q1)\cdot I2(I1+Q1)⋅I211 (held)0011 (held)0

Step 2 — find the logic. Q1 is never ON while I2 is OFF (in t3–t4, the interval bracketed by the dashed mark on the paper, I1 is ON but Q1 stays OFF), so I2 must be in series with the coil. Q1 comes ON when both I1 and I2 are ON (at 0 and at t4) and stays ON after I1 goes OFF (t1–t2 and t5–t6) until I2 goes OFF. That is a start-and-hold (latch) circuit: I1 starts, a Q1 holding contact in parallel with I1 keeps the output on, and I2 (normally open, must stay ON) acts as the enable/stop condition:

Q1=(I1+Q1)⋅I2Q1=(I1+Q1)\cdot I2Q1=(I1+Q1)⋅I2

Step 3 — check: the last row of the table reproduces the given Q1 output in every interval. Operation of the rung: when I1 and I2 are both ON, coil Q1 energises and its normally open contact Q1 closes, bypassing I1; Q1 therefore stays ON when I1 is released and switches OFF only when I2 opens; I1 alone (with I2 OFF) cannot switch Q1 on.

Note
The chart has no time scale, and in every interval Q1 also equals I2, so the single rung ─| I2 |──( Q1 )─ reproduces the chart as well. The latch rung above is the answer that uses both inputs, as the question intends; both give exactly the plotted output.

2022 · Q4(c)What is the function of optoisolator in PLC? 05Topic: optoisolator

An optoisolator (optocoupler) consists of an LED and a phototransistor (or photo-triac) in one package, coupled only by light (Fig. 7.2). In a PLC it is placed in every input and transistor/triac output channel. Its functions:

  1. Electrical isolation: the field circuit (24 V DC, 120/230 V AC, long cables) and the CPU's 5 V logic have no wired connection, so high voltages, spikes and faults in the field cannot reach and damage the CPU.
  2. Noise and surge protection: electrical noise, transients from inductive loads and ground loops are blocked; only the intended ON/OFF signal is transferred.
  3. Level conversion: the input current through the LED (from a 24 V or rectified AC signal) switches the phototransistor, which delivers a clean logic-level signal to the CPU (and vice versa for outputs).

Operation: when the field switch closes, current flows through the LED, which emits infrared light; the light switches on the phototransistor, giving a logic 1 to the processor. When the switch opens, the LED goes off and the CPU sees logic 0.

Source lectureNot in the slides of Asief Sir — PLC is a Section B topic (Priyo Sir, 1.Automation.pptx, slides 6–8; Bolton ch. 1); answer built from standard theory (see §7.3 of this book)
2022 · Q4(d)Explain the operation of the following input and output devices: (i) Magnetic read switch (ii) Solenoid 10Topic: reed switch · solenoid

(i) Magnetic reed switch (“read” on the paper = reed) — an input device used as a proximity switch (Fig. 7.3, left).

  • Construction: two thin, flexible, overlapping strips (reeds) of ferromagnetic material (nickel–iron), with plated contact tips, sealed in a glass envelope filled with inert gas; the reeds are separated by a small gap.
  • Operation: when a permanent magnet (or an energised coil) comes close, the reeds are magnetised with opposite polarities at their overlapping ends, attract each other and close the contact (normally-open type). When the magnet moves away the magnetic field disappears, the elasticity of the reeds separates them, and the contact opens. Changeover and normally closed versions also exist.
  • Connection to a PLC: the switch is wired to a digital input (24 V DC); closed = 1, open = 0.
  • Uses: door and guard interlocks (magnet in the door, switch in the frame), piston position sensing on pneumatic cylinders (magnet in the piston), float level switches, speed sensing.
  • Features: no physical contact with the moving part, hermetically sealed contacts (long life, clean), cheap; but limited current, some contact bounce, sensitive to stray magnetic fields.

(ii) Solenoid — an output device (actuator) that produces linear motion (Fig. 7.3, right).

  • Construction: a coil of insulated copper wire wound on a bobbin, with a movable soft-iron plunger (armature) partly inside it and a return spring.
  • Operation: when the PLC output energises the coil, the current produces a magnetic field that pulls the iron plunger into the coil (minimising the reluctance of the magnetic path), giving a linear stroke and force. When the current is switched off, the field collapses and the spring pushes the plunger back.
  • Use in a solenoid valve: the plunger moves a spool or poppet of a directional control valve; e.g. in a 3/2 or 5/2 solenoid valve, energising the solenoid connects the supply port to the cylinder port and the cylinder extends; de-energising lets the spring return the spool, venting the cylinder so it retracts. Solenoids also operate door locks, relays and contactors.
  • PLC interfacing: driven from a relay or transistor (DC) / triac (AC) output; a free-wheeling diode (DC) or RC snubber (AC) suppresses the voltage spike when the inductive coil is switched off.
